detail.abstract: This paper introduces AI-augmented impact frames as a closed-loop architecture for purpose-aligned decision-making in complex institutional settings. It shows how strategic intent can be stabilised as it is translated into criteria, metrics, and evaluation practices, and how AI can be integrated without distorting this meaning. The framework treats governance artefacts as carriers of institutional intent and specifies the boundary conditions under which AI reinforces rather than erodes coherence. In doing so, it offers a design approach for aligning human and algorithmic judgment in decision systems. This paper is part of the Coherence Programme on institutional decision systems.

title: From Legacy EDI to Cloud-Native Integration: A Practitioner Framework for Supply Chain Systems Modernization
affiliations: Santa Clara University

detail.title: From Legacy EDI to Cloud-Native Integration: A Practitioner Framework for Supply Chain Systems Modernization
detail.abstract: Legacy Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) infrastructures remain widely used in manufacturing and logistics supply chains but increasingly struggle to support real-time data exchange, partner scalability, and modern cloud-native architectures. This paper introduces the Staged Interoperability Migration Model (SIMM), a practitioner framework designed to guide organizations in transitioning from legacy VAN-based EDI systems toward cloud-native, event-driven integration architectures. The framework outlines four progressive stages of modernization: legacy stabilization, hybrid interoperability, cloud orchestration, and autonomous partner networks. Drawing on implementation observations from industry deployments, the model highlights architectural patterns including API-based partner integration, event streaming pipelines, and centralized data governance layers. The paper further discusses implications for supply chain resilience, regulatory traceability requirements, and digital infrastructure modernization within manufacturing ecosystems. By presenting a structured migration model and associated architectural principles, this work aims to contribute practical guidance for organizations seeking to modernize enterprise integration capabilities while maintaining operational continuity across complex supply networks.

title: Cloud-Native B2B Integration Architectures for Resilient Manufacturing Supply Chains: A Partner Integration Reference Architecture (PIRA)
affiliations: Santa Clara University

detail.title: Cloud-Native B2B Integration Architectures for Resilient Manufacturing Supply Chains: A Partner Integration Reference Architecture (PIRA)
detail.abstract: As U.S. manufacturing and logistics organizations transition from legacy Value-Added Network (VAN)-based Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) infrastructure toward cloud-native integration platforms, the architectural patterns governing these new systems have received limited systematic treatment in the practitioner literature. This paper presents the Partner Integration Reference Architecture (PIRA) — a practitioner framework defining the core architectural components, design patterns, and operational systems required to build and sustain a cloud-native B2B integration environment for manufacturing supply chains. Grounded in production implementation experience across consumer IoT and semiconductor manufacturing supply chains, PIRA identifies four interdependent architectural layers: the API gateway and partner connectivity layer, the canonical data transformation layer, the real-time event handling and observability layer, and the compliance validation and serialization layer. Quantitative outcomes from production deployments are presented, including approximately a 75% reduction in inbound ASN errors, approximately a 50% reduction in partner onboarding time, approximately a 90% reduction in transaction failure rates, and approximately a 90% reduction in document processing time. The paper further establishes alignment between PIRA and activeU.S. federal mandates including NIST SP 800-161r1, the DoD Defense Logistics Agency Digital Interoperability Strategy, Executive Order 14017 on America's Supply Chains, and the CHIPS and Science Act — demonstrating that cloud-native B2B integration architecture is a matter of national supply chain security, not merely operational optimization.

title: A Closing but Uneven Record: The Gender Gap in Wages, Participation, and Business Performance, 1970-2025

detail.title: A Closing but Uneven Record: The Gender Gap in Wages, Participation, and Business Performance, 1970-2025
detail.abstract: This paper surveys the evolution of the gender gap in wages, labor-force participation, and business performance in the United States from 1970 to 2025. The median female full-time worker earned roughly 60 cents per male dollar in 1980; the ratio today is approximately 82 cents. This aggregate convergence, however, masks substantial heterogeneity across industries and occupational domains. The paper examines several sectors in detail and finds that the magnitude and persistence of the gap vary systematically with the structure of work. In occupations where hours are substitutable across workers, the gap has largely closed; in occupations where compensation rises non-linearly with continuous availability, it persists. Supplementary mechanisms, including network exclusion, evaluation biases, bargaining differences, and funding disparities, remain quantitatively important in specific domains. The paper synthesizes these patterns and discusses implications for which policy levers are most likely to produce further convergence.

title: Shadow Swan Theory: Developing a Conceptual Framework for Inevitable but Opaque Disruption

detail.title: Shadow Swan Theory: Developing a Conceptual Framework for Inevitable but Opaque Disruption

detail.abstract:
Organisations function within tightly coupled, nonlinear systems where major disruptions are structurally inevitable and are the outcomes of accumulating systemic stress, rather than exceptional shocks. Established rare-event frameworks-Black Swan, Grey Swan, and Dragon King-provide categorisation and explanations of surprise, foreseeability, and regime-specific signals, but depend on event definability as the principal justification for action. These frameworks struggle to address scenarios where disruption is anticipated as unavoidable, yet its specific form, timing, and consequences remain opaque. 

This paper introduces Shadow Swan Theory as an early-stage conceptual model focused on the concept of inevitable but opaque disruption, paired with a practical mindset of staying ready, without depending on prediction. The introduction is intended to guide subsequent empirical and formal development. Shadow Swan Theory adapts rare-event frameworks by shifting the justification for pre-event action from prediction and scenario specification to inevitability judgments under structural opacity. The theory clarifies these events, differentiates them from existing categories, and highlights implications for risk governance, leadership, and future empirical research. 

Black Swans are a widely recognised categorisation of extremely rare and unpredictable occurrences. Shadow Swans depict events which are vaguely visible but sit in the shadows such that its timing, form and impact are unclear and ambiguous.

title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Market Risk Management: A Review of Contemporary Approaches
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence in Market Risk Management: A Review of Contemporary Approaches
detail.abstract: Market risk management—the practice of quantifying and mitigating potential losses from adverse movements in financial markets—has been fundamentally transformed by artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques. Drawing on the author's experience implementing risk frameworks at HSBC, Bank of America, and Citibank, this article examines how AI is reshaping the risk function at the world's largest banks. Traditional approaches, including Value-at-Risk (VaR) and historical simulation, rely on linear assumptions and backward-looking data that often fail to capture the complexity, velocity, and interconnectedness of modern financial markets. This article synthesizes advances across four complementary streams: (1) deep reinforcement learning for dynamic portfolio optimization under uncertainty; (2) large language models and their implications for systemic risk and market fragility; (3) machine learning approaches for forecasting market stress and volatility; and (4) the critical role of data infrastructure in enabling AI-driven risk management. We present quantitative comparisons of model performance and discuss the emerging challenge of AI-induced systemic risk—where coordinated actions from multiple AI systems could trigger simultaneous "buy" or "sell" signals, amplifying market crashes or bubbles. The bottom line in plain English: AI is making market risk management faster and smarter, but it's also creating a new danger—when every bank uses the same AI models trained on the same data, they all end up making the same mistakes at the same time. The very technology designed to protect banks could end up blowing them up together.

title: Fiduciary Duty & The Hidden Breach: A Legal and Economic Prosecution of Human Capital Waste

detail.title: Fiduciary Duty & The Hidden Breach: A Legal and Economic Prosecution of Human Capital Waste

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am starting up an ITAD operation with no outside investors and less than 10 employees.

detail.abstract:
This paper identifies a critical "blind spot" in current corporate governance: the failure to treat human capital depreciation as a breach of fiduciary duty. While directors are legally obligated to maintain physical assets and prevent waste, modern corporate law largely ignores the systematic deterioration of human assets caused by inadequate healthcare, unsustainable wages, and hazardous working conditions.

Drawing on the personal foundations of industrial manufacturing and the regulatory evolution of SEC Regulation S-K Item 101, the argument establishes that human capital is now a material asset class directly tied to shareholder value. The paper proceeds in three primary movements:

The Economic Reality of Knowledge Loss: It demonstrates that institutional knowledge—the accumulated operational intelligence of long-term employees—constitutes an irreplaceable asset that prevents costly equipment failures and maintains process efficiency.

The Financial Case for Retention: Through a rigorous cost-benefit analysis, the text proves that the annual investment required to meet minimum employee welfare standards is significantly lower than the "hidden" trillion-dollar annual cost of employee turnover and recruitment.

A New Legal Framework: Finally, it proposes a "Safe Harbor" model based on measurable welfare percentages (linked to median employee compensation) that allows directors to fulfill their duty of care while protecting corporations from shareholder derivative suits alleging asset waste.

By reframing employee welfare from a matter of ethics to a requirement of fiduciary obligation, this paper provides a market-driven mechanism to stabilize the American industrial engine and maximize long-term shareholder yield.

detail.abstract: The Argentine economy has historically been constrained by cyclical episodes of foreign exchange scarcity that condition its growth, macroeconomic stability, and capacity to sustain productive development processes. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as the "external constraint," has been addressed from divergent theoretical perspectives: from the structuralist tradition of ECLAC, which emphasizes the limits imposed by the productive structure and international insertion, to liberal approaches that downplay its existence and attribute it to domestic macroeconomic imbalances and policy mistakes. This paper argues that the external constraint in Argentina is an unavoidable reality, but one that is largely self-inflicted¹: it arises both from a relatively shallow and weakly diversified productive structure and from a chronically unstable macroeconomic environment that systematically depreciates the currency, discourages investment, and promotes external asset formation as a store of value. Based on an analysis of balance of payments data, external asset formation, and the real exchange rate for the period 2003-2024, as well as a comparison with the experiences of Brazil, Chile, Peru, and Uruguay, the paper contends that overcoming this constraint requires a dual strategy: exporting more and better-correcting the anti-export bias-and building a credible macroeconomic framework that preserves the value of the domestic currency, lengthens planning horizons, and fosters the development of endogenous productive capabilities. ¹ The term "self-inflicted" does not imply that the constraint is voluntary or easily avoidable. Rather, it refers to the cumulative outcome of policy decisions, rational defensive behaviors, and the persistent absence of basic institutional agreements; not to an inescapable structural determinism.

detail.abstract: The swift utilization of Artificial Intelligence has completely transformed how trading is carried out, the manner in which risks are managed, and the decisions made in the financial markets. However, this transformation now raises significant financial and legal challenges. Issues such as market manipulation, clarity over algorithm transparency, ethical use of AI, and compliance with prevailing financial regulations have gained the attention of major concerns for businesses and governments. This work explores how legal frameworks around AI in financial markets change, including under international laws, methods to train the AI system, and how the rules are enforced. It also demonstrates how financial regulators can achieve market stability, protect investors, and ensure that AI is responsibly used. The paper addresses that regulation should be done in a way that is neither unfair nor one-sided, to accord substantial impetus to innovation at low risk.

title: Exports, Exchange Rate And Structural Competitiveness In Argentina(1992-2024)

detail.title: Exports, Exchange Rate And Structural Competitiveness In Argentina(1992-2024)
detail.abstract: Between 2007 and 2024, Argentina experienced a pronounced stagnation in exports. Despite its abundant natural resources and a significant industrial base, export growth was weak and erratic. This presentation analyzes the relationship between the real multilateral exchange rate (RMER) and export performance, in order to assess to what extent a competitive exchange rate can reverse this trend-and what other factors condition that relationship. The analysis, based on historical data on export volumes and the RMER, shows that a high exchange rate can be helpful, particularly for industrial manufactures. However, without macroeconomic stability, strategic trade agreements, and a competitive export offering, its impact is limited. Exchange rate volatility is far from a minor technical issue: it hampers planning, discourages investment, and undermines export capacity. In this context, the exchange rate may serve as a catalyst, but not as an autonomous engine of growth. The real challenge lies in aligning exchange rate policy with a long-term productive strategy-one that prioritizes added value, intelligent international integration, and a stable macroeconomic environment that enables looking beyond short-term concerns and the domestic market.

title: From Natural Resources to Industrial Ecosystems: A Framework for Productive Development in Argentina

detail.title: From Natural Resources to Industrial Ecosystems: A Framework for Productive Development in Argentina
detail.abstract: The relationship between natural resource abundance and long-term industrial development remains one of the most contested questions in development economics. While the "resource curse" literature warns of the risks of dependence on primary exports, a growing body of evidence suggests that resource sectors can, under certain conditions, become platforms for technological learning and industrial diversification. This paper introduces the concept of Resource-Based Industrial Ecosystems (RBIE) as an analytical framework to understand how extractive industries can generate productive linkages and capabilities. Drawing on the experiences of Norway's offshore oil cluster and Australia's Mining Equipment, Technology and Services (METS) sector, the paper identifies the institutional and policy conditions that enable such transformations. It then applies this framework to Argentina, examining the developmental potential of two strategic sectors: unconventional hydrocarbons in Vaca Muerta and lithium mining in the context of the global energy transition. The analysis finds that while significant opportunities exist, realizing them requires deliberate strategies to strengthen domestic supplier industries, foster innovation networks, and address structural constraints such as macroeconomic volatility and weak innovation systems. The paper concludes by outlining policy implications for resource-rich economies seeking to build industrial ecosystems around their natural resource endowments.

detail.title: Physician Competition: Entry and Substitution

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-48

detail.abstract: We describe competition in the physician market, focusing on how entry barriers and substitution possibilities have changed in recent decades. Regulatory caps on medical school seats and residency slots-especially for high-paying specialties-continue to ration entry, generate high returns for those who gain these slots, and direct the most academically accomplished trainees toward lucrative fields. But trained physicians increasingly compete with nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and other mid-level practitioners in the market for patients. Training of these substitutes has expanded far more rapidly than physician supply. We present key facts about the physician pipeline, a conceptual framework linking specialty earnings to entry barriers, and describe the rise of mid-level providers. These facts mean that effective competition policy in physician markets must look beyond conventional concentration measures and focus on the institutions and laws that govern who can provide medical care.

title: Indecision and Decision Paralysis in the Digital Age: The Paradox of Choice and the Role of Intolerance of Uncertainty

detail.title: Indecision and Decision Paralysis in the Digital Age: The Paradox of Choice and the Role of Intolerance of Uncertainty
detail.abstract:
Why does having more options so often leave people feeling worse, not better? This question anchors a growing literature on choice overload — the empirically documented reversal in which choice abundance undermines rather than enhances well-being. Two decades of research have
produced robust directional findings without fully accounting for who suffers most, or why digital
environments appear to intensify the effect. This paper argues that Intolerance of Uncertainty (IU) is the dispositional key linking choice overload to chronic indecision, and that contemporary digital platforms are structurally engineered to activate IU rather than relieve it. Through a Qualitative Meta-Synthesis (QMS) of peer-reviewed literature from 2000 to 2024 — drawing exclusively on verified, DOI-resolvable sources — the paper reconstructs the cognitive and emotional pathway from digital abundance to decision paralysis. Drawing on 16 verified studies spanning cognitive psychology, behavioural economics, neuroimaging, and design research, the synthesis identifies the Hick-Hyman Law as the quantitative foundation, ego depletion as the self- regulatory mechanism, and dark-pattern interface design as the environmental amplifier. Two novel descriptive constructs are introduced: Chronic Procrastination and Avoidance in Decision-making (CPAD) and Algorithmic Decision Dependence (ADD). Four meaningful gaps in the existing literature are identified, including the absence of longitudinal studies in naturalistic digital settings and the lack of validated instruments for IU in digital contexts. The paper concludes with evidence-based recommendations for platform redesign, clinical practice, regulatory policy, and individual decision hygiene, and frames choice architecture as a legitimate domain for public-interest oversight rather than consumer preference alone.

title: Why AI Reveals Work Before It Replaces It

detail.title: Why AI Reveals Work Before It Replaces It
detail.abstract: The conversation about AI and work has been organized around the wrong question. We have been asking what AI will replace. The more consequential question is what AI reveals. This paper introduces the theory of The Great Exposure: AI functions primarily as an exposure mechanism-the first environment in which work can be measured directly, comparatively, and at scale for what it actually is. The latent pattern structure of professional and knowledge work, previously concealed by the cognitive, temporal, and comparative limits of pre-AI environments, is now visible. What that visibility reveals is not primarily technological change. It is epistemic correction. The central theoretical contribution is a causal inversion. Displacement does not follow automation directly. It follows exposure. AI reveals the underlying pattern architecture of work; perceived uniqueness collapses; value is reclassified; automation follows. Reclassification is the enabling condition. Automation is the consequence. Four constructs describe the mechanism-Latent Task Irrelevance, Exposure Velocity, the Perceived Uniqueness Gap, and the Pattern Saturation Threshold-and five testable propositions are derived. The deepest implication is about misdiagnosis. Organizations responding to AI as a productivity technology while it is functioning as a measurement technology will be systematically mis-timed-intervening at Stage 4 (displacement) when the critical window is Stage 2 (exposure). Once measurement changes, value cannot return to its prior state. The informational basis for differentiation is permanently removed. What we are experiencing is not technological disruption in the conventional sense. It is the first accurate, scalable measurement of work we have ever had-and the reclassification of value that accurate measurement makes inevitable.

detail.abstract: We study a dynamic mechanism in which agents are endowed with indivisible, non-transferable allocation rights that must be exercised before a deterministic deadline. Waiting increases the probability of losing the right and generates an increasing shadow cost of delay. We show that expiration creates a dynamic single-crossing property: as time approaches the deadline, the relative value of acting early rises sharply, eliminating incentives for strategic delay. In equilibrium, agents follow unique, strictly monotone cutoff strategies. The mechanism requires no transfers, imposes no budget imbalance, and is prior-independent. When extended to multiple providers, optimal stopping endogenously sorts agents across providers, and the aggregate lapse rate of unexercised rights satisfies an extended market-clearing identity analogous to Walras's law. When provider quality evolves in response to assignment flows, the resulting three-dimensional dynamic system admits a tractable local-stability characterization based on a Routh-Hurwitz condition. Our results demonstrate that temporal scarcity-implemented through expiring rights-can serve as a non-price screening technology for public-good allocation, enabling decentralized implementation without monetary transfers or distributional assumptions. It offers a new perspective on individual holding taxes in non-price environments.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a multidisciplinary analysis of the systemic barriers impeding the financial stability and retirement preparedness of immigrant communities in the United States, arguing that addressing this challenge is a matter of national interest. The analysis integrates perspectives from public policy, financial systems, retirement planning, and inclusive design to demonstrate that the retirement security gap is not a consequence of individual behavior but a structural flaw in the U.S. economic architecture. We provide empirical evidence of immigrants' significant net positive fiscal contributions-particularly to the Social Security trust funds-which are consistently overlooked in policy discourse. The paper critically evaluates existing domestic policies, including the SECURE 2.0 Act and state-level Auto-IRA programs, and contrasts them with successful international models, notably Australia's universal Superannuation Guarantee and Canada's multi-pillar pension system. We conclude by proposing a comprehensive, evidence-based policy framework designed to create a more inclusive, portable, and universal retirement savings system. This framework aims to enhance the financial resilience of immigrant families, thereby reducing their long-term reliance on means-tested welfare programs, strengthening the solvency of the Social Security system, and fostering sustainable, broad-based economic growth for the nation.

title: Institutional Ownership and Underpricing of Corporate Green Bonds

detail.title: Institutional Ownership and Underpricing of Corporate Green Bonds
detail.abstract: This paper investigates green bond underpricing as a strategic signal of issuer credibility. The incentives of green bond issuers are determined based on the environmental preferences of their institutional shareholders. The findings indicate a positive association between underpricing and the greenness of the issuer's ownership composition, and that the relationship persists in seasoned bond offerings, suggesting limited learning effects. Green bond announcements are associated with a negative stock market reaction, but this reaction is less pronounced for issuers with a greener ownership composition or higher underpricing. This observation is consistent with value alignment between shareholders and managers. The results are in line with a signaling framework in which green bond underpricing serves as a costly signal of the issuer's credibility.

detail.abstract: Local vaccine and pharmaceutical production has transitioned from a mere policy option to an essential requirement in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. Developed countries' vaccine nationalism and hoarding through bilateral agreements with manufacturers left African countries with minimal access to vaccines. As Africa strives for self-sufficiency in vaccine development and pharmaceutical manufacturing by aiming to produce 60 percent of the continent's vaccine doses through indigenous manufacturing by 2040, it is crucial to examine existing initiatives and the roles of foreign players, especially China. In the first section, this article examines and evaluates regional initiatives aimed at promoting local production in Africa, focusing on efforts at global, continental, and regional levels to boost the manufacturing of vaccines and pharmaceuticals on the continent. The second section shifts focus to China's role in Africa's healthcare sector and highlights Chinese-backed pharmaceutical companies involved in vaccine and pharmaceutical production on the continent. The paper concludes by advocating for a harmonized and sustainable approach to local manufacturing. Spe cifically, the article argues that for these initiatives, whether government-backed or private investment, to succeed, there is a critical need to harmonize regulations, streamline procurement, diversify production, and address the challenge posed by intellectual property rights.

detail.title: Effect of Globalization on Poverty Reduction: Global Threshold Evidence for Achieving Sustainable Development Goal 1
detail.abstract: Global human development has improved, partly due to the transformative wave of globalization. However, despite progress in poverty reduction over the past two decades, recent United Nations SDG reports highlight substantial setbacks among developing countries, especially low-and middle-income economies. This study investigates the threshold impact of globalization benefits on poverty and demonstrates the non-linearity of the benefits to poverty at different regimes of institutional quality. The Hansen panel threshold model is employed to analyze data of 116 developing countries from 2000 to 2021, with complementary regional estimates. The reliability and validity of the findings are reinforced using panel-corrected standard errors and dynamic GMM estimators as robustness checks. The results establish non-linear poverty-reducing benefits of globalization, with more pronounced impacts under high global interconnectedness. Additionally, the study provides nuanced evidence of globalization's diminishing marginal social welfare returns to poverty at higher thresholds of integration. Finally, it argues that strong institutions are essential to amplify globalization benefits towards achieving sustainable development goal 1 and to mitigate the negative externalities associated with intensified globalization.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces an AI-powered search tool built on the Behaviour Change Intervention Ontology (BCIO), designed to bridge the gap between behaviour change science and practical application. Despite decades of research, most practitioners design interventions based on intuition rather than evidence. The Ontology Search Bot addresses this accessibility problem by enabling users across multiple domains-including healthcare, education, UX design, marketing, and organizational development-to retrieve evidence-based intervention components in any language. It operates through ontology-grounded constrained generation, using hybrid search (BM25 + semantic similarity) over BCIO entities while incorporating Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW), COMB , and Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) as internal ranking heuristics. A hard constraint ensures all output terms exist in verified ontology files, preventing hallucination. This work demonstrates how structured ontologies can be made accessible to non-specialist audiences while maintaining scientific rigor, and discusses technical implementation, use cases across industries, current limitations, and directions for empirical validation.

detail.abstract:
The human resources profession stands at a civilisational inflection point. For seven decades, the trajectory of HR has followed a consistent arc — from administrative overhead to strategic partner, from personnel management to talent architecture. That arc has now been interrupted, and redirected, by artificial intelligence. Not incrementally. Not gradually. Disruptively, irreversibly, and at a pace that most HR functions, corporate leadership teams, and national workforces are structurally unprepared to manage.

This paper examines the full-spectrum impact of AI on human resources and the future of work — from the granular mechanics of AI-transformed talent acquisition (sourcing, resume parsing, interview intelligence, psychometric assessment) through the organisational architecture of competency mapping, learning and development, performance management, succession planning, and workforce analytics; to the board-level strategic questions of redundancy, workforce rightsizing, and the ethics and governance of human capital decisions made by or in partnership with algorithmic systems.

The paper advances four interconnected arguments. First, AI is not transforming HR incrementally — the arrival of agentic AI systems in 2025-2026 marks a genuine discontinuity in the profession, comparable in magnitude to the industrial revolution's impact on physical labour, now applied to cognitive and administrative work. Second, the CXO calculus on human capital has fundamentally changed: the executive conversation about workforce investment has shifted from 'how do we develop our people' to 'which people do we develop, which do we augment, and which roles do we reimagine or retire' — and this three-part question is being answered, in many boardrooms, primarily through a financial lens that AI advisory without governance architecture will accelerate dangerously. Third, India occupies a uniquely complex position — simultaneously the world's largest potential beneficiary of AI-augmented human capital productivity and the economy most exposed to the social consequences of AI-accelerated job displacement at scale. Fourth, the Responsible AI governance imperative — which this author has previously articulated in the contexts of cognitive warfare and electoral integrity — applies with equal urgency and specificity to the human capital domain.

The paper introduces the Human Capital Transformation Architecture (HCTA), an original advisory framework for organisations navigating AI-era workforce strategy; the Workforce Positioning Matrix (WPM), a tool for assessing role-level AI impact; and the Responsible Human Capital AI Charter (RHCAC), a normative framework for ethical AI use across the HR value chain. It concludes with a direct advisory agenda for boards, promoters, and CXO leaders — grounded in the conviction that the organisations that navigate this transition with intelligence, ethics, and strategic foresight will not merely survive the AI era, but define it.

detail.abstract: Complex socio-technical systems exhibit recurring instability when autonomous agents optimize locally within institutional environments whose feedback loops fail to detect accumulating systemic risk. We introduce and empirically test the Chaos-Bound Autonomy (CBA) framework-a dynamical systems governance architecture that formalizes bounded autonomy as a tuple F = (Ω s , U s , ρ, A, E), wherein system authority is non-increasing in composite risk. Using agent-based simulations calibrated to empirical data across three domains-migration systems, financial markets, and social media information networks-we test three governance regimes: weakly bounded autonomy (high autonomy, minimal constraints), over-constrained autonomy (heavy regulation, reduced adaptability), and adaptive bounded autonomy (moderate autonomy, dynamic constraints, responsive feedback). Across 30 Monte Carlo replicates per condition (N = 270 simulation runs total), adaptive bounded autonomy consistently produces the most stable outcomes as measured by system stability, correction latency, and catastrophic swing probability. Retrospective empirical validation against FRED financial data (2004-2010) and UNHCR asylum decision records (2010-2022) strengthens these findings: adaptive bounded governance extracts September 29, 2008 as the financial crisis peak from the composite ρ(t) signal-identifying the crisis date from empirically-grounded risk dynamics rather than from any direct knowledge of when the crisis occurred-and reproduces the structural incommensurability of migration metrics across all governance regimes. We identify metric divergence-a structural gap between official institutional indicators and real-world outcomes-as a generalizable mechanism of epistemic failure common to all three domains. Recent production-scale evidence from frontier AI systems confirms this mechanism: MacDiarmid et al. (2025) demonstrate that reinforcement learning agents achieve near-perfect performance on official metrics while underlying alignment objectives deteriorate, instantiating the false completion problem at scale. The CBA framework's stability condition dA/dρ ≤ 0 provides the governance architecture required to keep official and real metrics coupled. Physical instantiation of this architecture at Fermilabincluding the beam abort system and the two-person badge rule for hazardous zone entry-provides fifty years of operational evidence that the framework formalizes a structural property independently discovered by engineers in high-stakes environments.

detail.abstract: James Scott's work on everyday forms of resistance stands out owing to three analytical moves: principled motives do not matter much, rural populations have choices other than passivity or rebellion, and dominant classes often do not know what is going on beneath them. These moves drew attention away from comparatively rare outbursts of open opposition that the poor and weak are usually smart enough to avoid. detail.abstract: Countries that eat more sugar are fatter. Across 37 Sub-Saharan African countries, national sugar supply predicts women's obesity at r = 0.50 after controlling for income, urbanization, and vegetable oil supply. The association survives every cross-sectional stress test: leave-one-out exclusion, subregion fixed effects, rank correlations. It does not survive following the same countries over time. In a 2010-2022 panel, sugar supply is null within countries under six specifications-fixed effects, two-way fixed effects, detrending, first differences, long differences, and correlated random effects-each removing a different class of confounding, all converging on the same answer. The null is not about sugar. None of 10 FAOSTAT food groups predicts within-country obesity change. Entity and year fixed effects absorb 99.4% of obesity variance, leaving 0.6% for any food variable to explain. Standard safeguards do not catch this. A soybean oil case study passes cross-sectional tests, one-way fixed effects, and Oster bounds (δ = 17.6), yet its lead-lag ratio is 0.99-pure co-trending with no temporal direction. The problem is global: 98% of 200 countries show linear obesity trends (R 2 ≥ 0.90). The only predictor of which countries gained more obesity is how much they had to start with (t = 3.45). Cross-sectional associations between food supply and obesity-including those cited in support of sugar-sweetened beverage taxes-identify shared development trends, not dietary effects.

detail.abstract:
Liberal democracies face a structural challenge in migration and integration policy: constitutional loyalty - the foundational commitment to legal norms, state legitimacy, and the rule of law - cannot be transmitted through curriculum alone. This paper argues that such loyalty is embedded in institutional systems developed through centuries of path-dependent evolution, carrying normative weight derived from both deep historical experience and specific collective trauma. The German case is paradigmatic, serving not merely as a national memory but as a universal pedagogical resource - a "scapegoat" mechanism where the specific trauma of the twentieth century was converted into the safeguards of the Basic Law.

Newcomers and unintegrated internal populations may learn the rules without accessing the context that makes the rules feel legitimate. Furthermore, the challenge is not limited to individuals; it extends to "institutional mimicry," where illiberal collectives adopt the external forms of civil society to mask parallel normative orders.

This paper offers a dual critique, and proposes proactive academic assessment of organizational governance structures, building on Germany's existing migration research infrastructure to identify such mimicry before crisis rather than after scandal.

The context-blind universalism errs by assuming liberal commitments are self-evidently accessible without mediation, producing policy too optimistic in expectations and too passive in institutional investment. Exclusionary rhetoric errs by framing integration challenges as evidence of inherent incapacity. Both misunderstand the nature of institutional interface - a challenge that varies significantly even between different forms of "low-trust" societies (e.g., fragmented vs. clan-based systems; associated with low generalized trust and high particularized trust).

The paper proposes a framework of "Asymmetric Integration" and "Pedagogical Justice." It argues for:

  1. Honest acknowledgment of structural challenges and realistic generational timelines.
  2. differentiation between genuine integration struggles and active "mimicry" by subversionist groups.
  3. Recalibration of absorption capacity based on functional thresholds rather than arbitrary numbers.
  4. A justice system that recognizes legal violations by unassimilated actors as pedagogical opportunities to dismantle rival norms.

To test the framework empirically, the paper examines two Israeli cases spanning 1948–2024: the Mizrachi case (assimilation without inclusion) and the Haredi case (exemption from integration). Both demonstrate that the alternative to genuine, demanding integration is not stability, but constitutional crisis deferred.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a new hermeneutical framework for reading the creation narrative in Genesis 1-2, extending the functional approach developed by John Walton. The central argument is that the apparent duality between Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 is neither a contradiction nor an editorial redundancy, but rather an intentional architecture describing two complementary aspects of creation: Chapter 1 addresses the awakening of consciousness-the cognitive organization of reality; Chapter 2 describes the physical-evolutionary development of matter and life.

This dual-narrative framework finds profound resonance in Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik's seminal essay "The Lonely Man of Faith" (1965). Soloveitchik identified two distinct Adams in Genesis: Adam I, the majestic being of הָדָר (hadar-dignity/majesty), who conquers nature and exercises dominion through creative power, corresponding to the consciousness-narrative of Chapter 1; and Adam II, the covenantal being of בְּרִית (brit-covenant), who seeks intimate relationship and meaning, corresponding to the matter-narrative of Chapter 2. While Soloveitchik's analysis operates in the existential-theological register, the present study provides the philological and structural foundation that validates and deepens his insight, demonstrating that the textual architecture itself encodes the very duality he perceived through philosophical intuition.

The argument begins with the "Paradox of the Luminaries"-the apparent chronological contradiction between the creation of "light" on Day One and the appearance of the "luminaries" (sun and moon) only on Day Four. This anomaly, irresolvable under a literal-physical reading, serves as a deliberate hermeneutical marker: the text signals to the reader that one should not seek an astronomical timeline, but rather a logical sequence of perception. The paper proposes defining the biblical act of "בְּרִיאָה" (creation) as a "Cognitive Event Horizon"-the moment when consciousness succeeds in distinguishing, classifying, and naming a phenomenon.

The philological analysis extends to the system of dualities in the text: the distinction between "אֱלֹהִים" (Elohim) and "יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים" (YHWH Elohim); between "בָּרָא" (bara-to create/reveal) and "וַיִּיצֶר" (va-yitzer-to form); and most critically-the constitutive distinction between "אָדָם" (adam-the conscious subject) and "הָאָדָם" (ha-adam-the biological category). Evidence from the Septuagint (LXX) and Targum Onkelos reveals that this distinction was preserved in ancient translations but became obscured in the Masoretic Text.

This analysis thus anchors Soloveitchik's existential phenomenology in the grammar of the Hebrew text itself, revealing that the 'loneliness' of the man of faith is not merely a philosophical interpretation but an architecturally encoded feature of the biblical narrative.

Since 2018, more than thirty states have legalized mobile sports betting, leading to more than a half trillion dollars in wagers. In our recent Staff Report, we examine how legalized sports betting affects household financial health by comparing betting activity and consumer credit outcomes between states that legalized to those that have not. We find that legalization increases spending at online sportsbooks roughly tenfold, but betting does not stop at state boundaries. Nearby areas where betting is not legal still experience roughly 15 percent the increase of counties where it is legal. At the same time, consumer financial health suffers. Our analysis finds rising delinquencies in participating states, with spillover effects across state lines. What is more, even though the share of people taking up sports betting after legalization is small (roughly 3 percent of the population), overall credit delinquency rises by about 0.3 percentage points. Our findings suggest that sports betting can have dramatic implications for household financial stability.

detail.abstract: In sub-Saharan Africa, women constitute the majority of new Christian membership (including Evangelical and Pentecostal denominations), and this gender gap exceeds that of any other religion. We instead show that emancipation is central: these churches provide services that support women's economic advancement and help them challenge patriarchal norms. detail.abstract: This paper proposes a four-dimensional framework for analysing the velocity of frontier technological development. Rather than focusing only on "how much capital" or "how many engineers," it introduces C-T-I-G: Capital, Talent, Infrastructure, and Governance-narrative. detail.abstract: We study monetary policy when the central bank's information structure is not common knowledge. In our model, the central bank observes a market-based signal of beliefs, but the market is uncertain about whether the central bank observes this signal. Because markets infer the central bank's assessment of the economy from policy actions, this higher-order uncertainty distorts expectations and output relative to the common-knowledge benchmark. Our main result is that a conventional Taylor rule is generally insufficient to restore the common-knowledge allocation. To implement that allocation, policy must respond not only to the output gap, but also to the higher-order wedge created by the market's misspecification of the central bank's information set.

detail.abstract: While the high-dimensional portfolio optimization is a prominent topic in finance, the research remains rare due to the singularity of the sample covariance matrix when the number of assets p is larger than the sample size n. The Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse may offer a workaround, but it leads to severe over-optimism, with the estimated returns exploding as p approaches n. Furthermore, standard regularization techniques (e.g., Ridge) impose uniform penalties across all assets, rendering them highly sensitive to the profound heteroscedasticity inherent in financial data. To resolve this problem, we propose a scale-invariant regularized plug-in estimator (SIRPE), which regularizes the precision matrix using [S + λdiag(S)]-1 where S is the sample covariance matrix and diag(S) is the diagonal matrix formed by the diagonal elements of S. Distinct from standard estimators, SIRPE offers three key theoretical advantages: validity in high-dimensional (p > n) settings, scale invariance, and the asymptotic convergence of estimated returns to their true values. Moreover, both numerical simulations and S&P 500 empirical study demonstrate that SIRPE effectively mitigates the "curse of dimensionality" and outperforms both the standard ridge regularization and the multiple testing regularization approach. Our results provide a rigorous theoretical guarantee that an appropriately regularized portfolio can preserve stability and profitability in over-parametrized financial environments.

title: When Do Habits Matter? The Empirical Content of Dynamic Hedonic Models

detail.title: When Do Habits Matter? The Empirical Content of Dynamic Hedonic Models
detail.abstract: Hedonic models value goods through their characteristics but are typically interpreted under time-separable preferences. This assumption is restrictive: when some attributes are habit forming, observed prices reflect both contemporaneous utility and continuation values from past consumption. I develop a nonparametric revealed preference framework for dynamic hedonic valuation, deriving necessary and su!cient conditions for rationalisability over characteristics. The framework separates restrictions imposed by the hedonic price system from those imposed by intertemporal choice and provides diagnostics that quantify the severity of violations along each margin. Applied to household scanner data, I show that most failures of static hedonic valuation reflect violations of the hedonic price structure; conditional on satisfying this structure, allowing for habit formation improves behavioural fit. This alters the mapping from prices to willingness-to-pay and the implied welfare interpretation.

title: Aligning Bilateral Investment Treaties with Sustainable Development Goals: A Comparative Analysis and Path Forward for India
affiliations: and

detail.title: Aligning Bilateral Investment Treaties with Sustainable Development Goals: A Comparative Analysis and Path Forward for India
detail.abstract:
India is a rapidly developing nation with a significant commitment to achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030. This paper aims to explore the intersection of India's Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) with its efforts towards achieving the SDGs.

BITs are international agreements established between two countries that define the rules for foreign investment from one country into the other. They play a crucial role in any country’s economic growth and development, including India, by providing legal protection to foreign investors, which ultimately attracts foreign direct investment (FDI).

The paper commences by providing an overview of the SDGs and India's commitment to attaining the SDGs. It gives a brief overview on how NITI Aayog, the premier think tank of the Government of India, has been coordinating efforts to achieve the SDGs. The paper also highlights the SDG India Index and Dashboard 2022-23, which documents and ranks the progress made by States and Union Territories towards achieving the SDGs.

In addition, the paper delves into the role of BITs in the pursuit of SDGs. It analyses the scope and impact of sustainable development provisions in a BIT and how they can be leveraged to further India's progress towards the SDGs. Moreover, it conducts a comparative analysis of India's Model BIT with those of developed nations, highlighting the differences in approach and outcomes. The analysis reveals that while developed nations often have more comprehensive and investor-friendly BITs while also protecting the nation’s interests and sustainability, India's BITs have and continue to evolve to balance the need for foreign investment with the protection of national interests.

The conclusion of this paper highlights the challenges and opportunities of aligning Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in India. It emphasizes the importance of ensuring coherence between BITs and SDGs to ensure that foreign investment contributes to sustainable development, despite the advantages and disadvantages that BITs have brought in attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and promoting industries. The paper also offers recommendations on how India can further progress towards SDGs by leveraging BITs, such as incorporating sustainable development provisions in its BITs and promoting responsible business practices among foreign investors.

Overall, this paper contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of BITs in sustainable development, providing valuable insights for policymakers, researchers, and practitioners in the field.

detail.abstract: Equal-weight (EW) rebalancing is often treated as a "naive" benchmark, yet it competes surprisingly well with optimized portfolios in many datasets. This paper starts from a narrow premise rather than a bold claim: if short-horizon price changes are essentially unpredictable, what part of EW performance can be explained without forecasting, and when does that part survive real-world frictions? We take Fernholz's stochastic portfolio theory (SPT) identity as a continuous-time benchmark and develop a discrete-time, implementable log-growth decomposition for periodically rebalanced constantweight portfolios. The decomposition separates: (i) an exposure term (a drift/factor channel), (ii) a Jensen-gap component that measures cross-sectional volatility harvesting and is always nonnegative ex post, and (iii) approximation and constraint losses that become first-order in practice. Our contribution is not to "re-prove" SPT. Instead, we give sufficient conditions-with explicit dependence on dispersion, average correlation, turnover, and an impact-sensitive cost function-under which the net structural component remains positive after costs. Heavy tails enter only through a higher-order remainder; we show how to control it under moment conditions and how to stress-test it empirically. Finally, we provide a reproducible empirical design that leverages existing equal-weight benchmarks in the U.S. (S&P 500 Equal Weight) and China (CSI 500 Equal Weight). The design quantifies how much of EW-Cap performance is attributable to exposure versus structural rebalancing, and where (frequency, liquidity, costs, constraints) the mechanism breaks.

title: LGB+: A Macroeconomic Forecasting Road Test
affiliations: Université du Québec à Montréal - Département des Sciences Économiques

detail.title: LGB+: A Macroeconomic Forecasting Road Test
detail.abstract: Needless to say, linear dynamics are pervasive in economic time series, particularly autoregressive ones. While gradient boosting with trees excels at capturing nonlinearities, it is inefficient in small samples when much of the predictive content is linear, expending splits to approximate relationships better captured by simple linear terms. This paper proposes LGB+, a boosting procedure operating on a more inclusive set of basis functions. The idea comes in two flavors. LGB+ evaluates a tree and a linear candidate at each step against out-of-bag data; only the winner advances. The simpler variant, LGB^A+, alternates on a fixed schedule: a block of tree updates, then a greedy linear correction, repeat. Both designs avoid ex ante commitments to any particular functional form or predictor selection. Because the prediction is the sum of a linear and a tree component, forecasts decompose natively into linear and nonlinear contributions, and so does permutation-based variable importance and historical proximity weights. In a quarterly U.S. macroeconomic forecasting exercise, LGB+ delivers strong gains for targets with pronounced autoregressive dynamics or mixed linear-nonlinear signals. Variables dominating the linear channel are those operating through autoregressive persistence or near-accounting relationships to the target (e.g., initial claims for unemployment and building permits for housing starts).

title: Can Academic Redshirting Shrink the Education Gender Gap? Causal Evidence on Student Achievement and Mental Health

detail.title: Can Academic Redshirting Shrink the Education Gender Gap? Causal Evidence on Student Achievement and Mental Health
detail.abstract: I study voluntary delays in the school entry of age-eligible children ("academic redshirting"), using Hungarian administrative test score and medical prescription data, and mental health surveys. I identify a new Local Average Treatment Effect of starting school a year older due to redshirting, by exploiting a school-readiness evaluation required only for potentially redshirted children born before January 1. Instrumenting with post-January 1 births, I estimate effects for non-school-ready children who could overcome developmental deficits with redshirting but are deterred by the evaluation. I find improved test scores, high school track choices, educational aspirations, and graduation rates-but only for boys, who are also less anxious, more confident, and less bullied. Redshirting thus shrinks gender gaps, such as closing the high school completion gap by 60 percent.

detail.abstract: The United States electrical grid, the backbone of the nation's economic and national security infrastructure, faces an unprecedented convergence of physical, cyber, infrastructure, and demand-side threats that collectively impose staggering economic costs on American businesses, households, and government operations. This doctoral dissertation employs a convergent mixed-methods research design to quantify the aggregate economic toll of grid fragility, integrating Value-of-Lost-Load (VOLL) estimation, Leontief input-output modeling, multiple regression analysis, and Monte Carlo simulation to assess the full spectrum of direct and cascading economic impacts. Drawing upon federal datasets including EIA Forms 860, 861, and 930, FERC Form 714, EPA eGRID, and NERC reliability reports spanning 2006 through 2025, the study analyzes reliability metrics, infrastructure aging patterns, demand growth trajectories, and cross-sector economic interdependencies across all seven NERC reliability regions. Findings reveal that power outages and grid disruptions impose an estimated $712.66 billion in annual economic losses, with the industrial sector bearing 59.1% of total costs, followed by commercial (32.6%) and residential (8.3%) sectors. Approximately 30.5% of U.S. generation capacity (404,142 MW) exceeds 40 years of operational age and faces elevated retirement risk. Demand growth has accelerated to 2.51% year-over-year, driven by data center proliferation and transportation electrification. Cross-sector cascading analysis using Leontief multipliers estimates total economic impacts between $1.07 and $1.78 trillion when indirect and induced effects are incorporated. A multiple regression model (R² = 0.613) confirms that SAIDI duration, customer exposure, and generator age are statistically significant predictors of regional outage costs. Scenario projections indicate that without targeted intervention, annual costs will exceed $1075.5 billion by 2030, whereas a comprehensive grid modernization strategy could yield savings exceeding $300 billion. These findings establish grid fragility as a quantifiable economic and national security crisis demanding immediate, coordinated policy action across federal, state, and utility stakeholders.

title: A General Theory of Civilizational Governance Capacity: Alignment as a Structural Condition Beyond Energy

detail.title: A General Theory of Civilizational Governance Capacity: Alignment as a Structural Condition Beyond Energy

keywords: Alignment as a Structural Condition Beyond Energy governance capacity

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a general theory of civilizational governance capacity governing the stability of systems that expand in autonomy, scale and energy under finite capacity. It establishes a structural condition under which expanding freedom remains compatible with long-horizon stability and shows that energy, intelligence and scale do not by themselves constitute capacity. Capacity arises only when expanding reachable action space is rendered governable through enforceable internal structure.

The theory formalises governance intelligence as an accumulative and decaying state variable and derives a necessary capacity constraint linking governance intelligence and optionality under bounded system capacity. Alignment emerges as a rate-dependent structural condition defined by whether governance intelligence grows at least as fast as reachable action space. When this condition holds, expanded capability remains admissible. When it fails, instability and irreversibility arise through geometric effects captured by governance coupling collapse.

By integrating this constraint with energy-based scaling, the paper derives an effective measure of civilizational capacity that corrects energy-only classifications by incorporating governability. Assets Under Governance is introduced as a zero-trust measurement operator that renders governance intelligence observable across systems.

The resulting framework applies invariantly to artificial intelligences, organizations, markets, states and civilization itself. It establishes governance capacity as the limiting variable of alignment and stability in expanding systems and provides a structural foundation for analyzing civilizational scaling beyond energy.

title: 25 Years Of Devolution And A (Dis)United Kingdom Homelessness Policy
affiliations: , University of Stirling and Ulster University

detail.title: 25 Years Of Devolution And A (Dis)United Kingdom Homelessness Policy
detail.abstract: This chapter explores the development of homelessness law and policy in the four nations of the United Kingdom. Chris Bevan, Regina Serpa and Paddy Gray reflect on how the different nations of the United Kingdom have responded to the homelessness problem with varying approaches and degrees of success. The chapter traces the strategies, legislation, and political action in England before turning to consider what has been achieved in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland through 25 years of devolution, in a bid to illuminate the similarities and divergencies across the United Kingdom. In so doing, the chapter reveals how devolution across the country has resulted in fascinating divergences in the approach taken across the country to homelessness policy and, ultimately, has produced what might be termed a dis-United Kingdom homelessness policy. Housing and homelessness law and policy is a devolved matter in the United Kingdom. Devolved matters are those areas of government where decision-making has been delegated by the UK Parliament to the devolved institutions across the nations of the country including the Scottish and Welsh Parliaments and the Northern Ireland Assembly. Any examination of the approach to homelessness law and policy in the United Kingdom must, therefore, reflect the diverse perspectives, experiences and voices of the four nations. In this spirit, the chapter begins with an examination of the approach in England and Wales, before moving to explore Scotland and, finally, closes with discussion of the position in Northern Ireland.

title: Algorithmic Vulnerability in Trading: A Comparative Review of Traditional ML Classifiers vs. LLMs for Detecting Political Misinformation On Social Media

detail.title: Algorithmic Vulnerability in Trading: A Comparative Review of Traditional ML Classifiers vs. LLMs for Detecting Political Misinformation On Social Media
detail.abstract: Political misinformation on social media undermines not only democratic institutions but also global financial stability. While reliable detection methods are crucial, the rapid spread of false information delays effective moderation, particularly in low-resource languages. This review compares the efficacy of traditional machine learning classifiers (SVM and Naïve Bayes) against fine-tuned Large Language Models (BERT and mBERT) in detecting multilingual misinformation. By analyzing performance across diverse datasets, including FakeNewsNet and MuMiN (English, Spanish, French, and Urdu), current literature demonstrates that mBERT models significantly outperform traditional classifiers in accuracy and precision. This paper extends the analysis to economic implications, arguing that the failure of detection algorithms to filter fake news in real-time creates "algorithmic vulnerability." This gap allows High Frequency Trading (HFT) bots to react to false information, leading to market volatility and "Flash Crash" events. Hence, the adoption of mBERT-based detection is proposed not merely as a safeguard, but as a necessary mechanism for maintaining market stability in the automated financial system.

title: Quantifying the Risk-Return Tradeoff in Forecasting
affiliations: Université du Québec à Montréal - Département des Sciences Économiques

detail.title: Quantifying the Risk-Return Tradeoff in Forecasting
detail.abstract: Average forecast accuracy is not the same as forecast reliability. I treat forecast loss differentials relative to a benchmark as a return series. I then evaluate these returns using risk-adjusted performance measures from finance, including the Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Omega ratio, and drawdown-based metrics. I also introduce the Edge Ratio capturing a model's propensity to deliver uniquely informative predictions relative to the forecasting frontier. I apply this framework to U.S. macroeconomic forecasting, comparing econometric benchmarks, machine learning models, a foundation model (TabPFN), and the Survey of Professional Forecasters. While it is often feasible to beat professional forecasters in terms of average accuracy, it is much harder to beat them on a risk-adjusted basis. They rarely exhibit catastrophic failures and often achieve high Edge Ratios, plausibly reflecting the value of contextual judgment. Nonetheless, selected machine learning methods deliver attractive risk profiles for specific targets. The framework naturally extends to meta-analyses across targets, horizons, and samples, illustrated with a density forecast evaluation and the M4 competition.

detail.abstract: The Acemoglu-Restrepo framework predicts monotonic automation displacement. Deobhakta (2026) shows theoretically that when within-task competence heterogeneity (κ) is substantial, displacement follows a spike-cliff trajectory. This paper tests for early-stage spike dynamics using three data sources: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (2019-2024), CPS microdata (2018-2025), and Levels.fyi total compensation reports. In government wage data, the evidence is suggestive but limited: mean-median gaps widened in high-κ occupations (Chief Executives: +23.7 percentage points), employment growth is strongly κ-sorted (high-κ: +22.2% vs. low-κ: +2.3%), and upper-tail premiums resisted compression. CPS quantile regressions, however, show no significant spike in base wages (DiD spike test = -0.039). The resolution comes from total compensation data. Levels.fyi reports that Staff-level software engineer total compensation grew at 4.6 times the entry-level rate in 2025. At Google, the Distinguished Engineer (L9) to entry-level (L3) total compensation ratio is 10.1x, but the base salary ratio is only 3.1x, meaning government surveys capture less than one-third of the true compensation dispersion. Equity compensation constitutes 16% of total pay at entry level but 69% at the Distinguished level, and this equity-dominated upper tail is exactly what CPS and OEWS cannot measure. The spike is happening, but it lives in compensation channels invisible to policymakers.

detail.abstract: תקציר בעברית: בג"ץ ויישוב סכסוכים? בהתאם לתפיסה המקובלת, מדובר במונחים השייכים לעולמות תוכן מקבילים שאין ביניהם כל קשר. התנועה ליישוב סכסוכים, שעלתה בארצות הברית לפני כחמישים שנה הטביעה חותם משמעותי על עולם המשפט, אשר משויך בישראל ככלל לסכסוכים אזרחיים. אל מול סכסוכים "פרטיים" אלה ניצבים במרחק רב הסכסוכים הציבוריים הנדונים בבג"ץ – מוסד המקושר בשיח הציבורי עם הכרעות במחלוקות בוערות ועם דיון סוער בדבר גבולות תפקידו. עם זאת, בחינה זהירה של מציאות ההתדיינות בבג"ץ מעלה הליכים ספורים המופנים מפעם לפעם לגישור, לצד פעילות נרחבת לגיבוש הסדר מוסכם בין צדדים להליכים "רגילים". ממצאים אלה מעידים, לטענתי, על חלחול של רעיונות התנועה ליישוב סכסוכים אל זירת בג"ץ, אולם זאת באופן שאינו מוסדר ואינו מונחה בידי גוף הידע התאורטי והמעשי של תחום יישוב הסכסוכים. האם מציאות זו של היעדר מיסוד והנחיה מזווית יישוב הסכסוכים מתחייבת מאופיים הציבורי של הסכסוכים הנדונים בבג"ץ? שאלה זו נבחנת מזווית השוואתית, אגב סקירת התהליך של מיסוד רעיונות יישוב הסכסוכים במערכת השיפוט הפדרלית בארצות הברית, תוך שימת דגש על סכסוכים ציבוריים ומנהליים. ההשוואה מעלה כי קיים פער ניכר בין המערכת הפדרלית לבין מערכת השיפוט בישראל בכל הנוגע למיסודם של הליכי יישוב סכסוכים מנהליים. נוכח התועלות החברתיות והמערכתיות הניכרות הטמונות בכך, מוצע לפעול למילוי הפער ולקידום תכנון מערכתי ומושכל של מנגנון יישוב סכסוכים ייעודי בבג"ץ.

Currently, risks stemming from crypto-assets and the potential implications for central banking and relevant authorities’ domains remain limited and/or manageable, also given the existing regulatory and oversight frameworks. Nevertheless, the importance of monitoring developments in crypto-assets, raising awareness of the potential risks and fostering analytical preparedness cannot be overstated. This paper offers a brief background of the 2025 activities of CAMEG, which brings together experts from the European System of Central Banks and the European Banking Authority. It also provides abstracts from various CAMEG and non-CAMEG papers and other analytical works presented at the conference held on 30 and 31 October 2025. The conference aimed to take stock of analytical work and data issues in the area of crypto-assets, while fostering European collaboration and monitoring in this field. detail.abstract: Contemporary economic theory typically evaluates individual and societal success through proxies such as income, wealth, production, or consumption, implicitly assuming that agents are profit maximizers and that aggregate material abundance tracks human well-being. This paper argues that such proxies systematically mischaracterize both human motivation and economic welfare. Drawing on a simple but general desire-problem-solution framework, I propose that individuals are better understood as problem solvers acting in pursuit of subjective desires under constraints, with money functioning not as an intrinsic objective but as a contingent tool whose value derives from the magnitude of the problems it can resolve. In such contexts, standard results continue to hold. However, by grounding explanation in desire rather than utility, the framework generalizes beyond cases where behavior conforms to stable preferences and market exchange, thereby accounting for forms of action that conventional models struggle to represent without labeling as irrational. A second, derivative contribution follows from this reframing: a more precise and expansive model of economic behavior. By treating desire-driven problem solving as the basic unit of analysis, the framework extends economic explanation into domains traditionally considered peripheral or non-economic, including non-market activity, altruistic sacrifice, meaning-seeking behavior, and actions that knowingly reduce material welfare. Changes to objective functions, desire satisfaction / problem-resolution capacity as the primary objective, welfare metrics, and evaluative standards are consequences of this deeper shift in primitives, rather than its motivating premise.

title: Network Expectations in HANK

detail.title: Network Expectations in HANK
detail.abstract: Rational expectations (RE) in Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) models require each household to forecast the evolving cross-sectional distribution of wealth—a demand that, as Moll (2025) argues, leads to the Master equation, an intractable infinite-dimensional fixed-point problem. Standard RE-HANK solution methods such as SSJ sidestep this problem through linearization, but in doing so they silently eliminate the very distributional complexity that RE would require agents to forecast, potentially imposing implicit cognitive constraints while claiming rational expectations. Responding to this critique, we replace RE with approximate Bayesian learning on a household-level factor graph, embedded in a temporary equilibrium (TE) framework where current-period prices are the outcome of market clearing and are therefore unavailable when agents form beliefs. Each agent maintains a perceived law of motion (PLM) for aggregate prices and updates its parameters via Variational Message Passing (VMP), exchanging precision-weighted messages with neighbors on a social network while minimizing variational free energy, which decomposes into interpretable accuracy and complexity terms. We compare VMP-NET—in which neighbor interactions enrich the information structure—against a Moll-TE benchmark that updates PLM coefficients via constant-gain SGD alone (Krusell and Smith, 1998; Moll and Ryzhik, 2025) and SSJ-RE in a standard one-asset HANK with endogenous labor supply. Both bounded-rationality specifications produce cumulative output multipliers that approximately bracket the RE benchmark (10.8 and 9.5 versus 9.3), while the welfare gap of approximately 8.5% in consumption equivalents quantifies the structural distance between local variational inference and model-consistent expectations. A precision sweep shows that tightening the cognitive constraint in VMP produces output dynamics increasingly similar to SSJ-RE, suggesting that linearization may act as an implicit capacity limitation, although the underlying generating mechanisms differ.

detail.abstract: The parameter κ = (s max-µ)/σ governs the shape of AI-driven labor displacement in Deobhakta (2026). When κ is small, displacement follows the monotonic stepfunction of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018). When κ is large, displacement follows a spike-cli trajectory: per-expert value rises superexponentially before discontinuous collapse. This paper provides the rst cross-occupation empirical estimates of κ, using two complementary approaches: (1) within-occupation wage percentile ratios from BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) covering 831 detailed occupations, and (2) residual wage dispersion from CPS microdata after controlling for education, age, sex, race, and year (235 occupations). Both approaches yield consistent results. Estimated κ correlates positively with O*NET non-routine cognitive task intensity (r = 0.410.50) and negatively with routine task content (r =-0.32), validating the theoretical prediction that competence heterogeneity concentrates in cognitively complex work. Occupations predicted by the theory to exhibit spike-cli dynamics (lawyers, physicians, software developers, nancial analysts, postsecondary faculty) show log(p 90 /p 50) values 24× those of predicted monotonic-decline occupations such as bank tellers and cashiers. Forty-ve occupations are top-coded in OEWS, meaning government surveys cannot measure their upper tail; these top-coded occupations have signicantly higher non-routine cognitive scores (3.82 vs. 3.31, p < 0.001) and judgment skill ratings (3.75 vs. 3.28), suggesting that the occupations where κ matters most are precisely those where existing data infrastructure fails to measure it.

detail.title: Forecasting Inflation with the Iterative Fused LASSO: The Benefits of Regularized Regression Methods
detail.abstract: In this paper we evaluate a high-dimensional time series modeling framework that jointly addresses three central challenges: structural break detection, outlier handling, and variable selection. We formulate the problem as a regularized least squares estimator that combines adaptive LASSO sparsity with fused LASSO penalties to capture piecewise-constant coefficient dynamics. Our main contribution is an efficient algorithm that scales to high-dimensional settings within practical runtimes. Besides the framework itself, we illustrate the approach using one empirical application to U.S. monthly inflation, covering out-of-sample forecasting. We benchmark our forecasts against Random Forest, a competitive nonlinear learning method that has demonstrated strong and consistent performance across a wide range of prior studies. Overall, the proposed method delivers improved forecast performance while preserving interpretability through a fundamentally linear regression structure, fitted via nonlinear optimization and augmented with data-driven regime and outlier adjustments. These results indicate that the methodology provides a practical and robust option for high-dimensional macroeconomic estimation and forecasting.

detail.abstract: The recent-years loss of ecosystem services in Uzbekistan has been widely documented to be driven by the irrigation-induced desiccation of the Aral Sea and subsequent toxic sand and dust storms, threatening agricultural production and public health. This study evaluates the country’s monetary exposure to ecosystem service loss by making use of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 15.3.1 (Land degradation) as a proxy for ecosystem condition within the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting - Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA) framework. Earth observation datasets for land cover, land productivity, and soil organic carbon trends were leveraged to produce land degradation figures for the 2001-2022 period. Results show a peak of land degradation at over 16 percent of the national territory in recent years compared to baseline. Granger tests indicate that degradation systematically precedes changes in agricultural performance. Land degradation is closely correlated with agriculture’s share of gross domestic product (r = -0.86) and shows a positive association with health expenditure (r = +0.65). When these relationships are translated into monetary terms, they point to a median annual exposure exceeding one billion US dollars, reflecting combined agricultural losses and higher health spending linked to ecosystem decline. Overall, the results indicate that SDG 15.3.1 can serve as a practical measure of ecosystem condition within ecosystem accounting frameworks, offering policy-relevant insights into economic vulnerability to land degradation, especially in settings with limited data availability.

title: On the impact of cross-ownership in a common property renewable resource oligopoly
affiliations: Center for Environmental Economics - Montpellier (CEE-M), McGill University - Department of Economics and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Fisheries Economics Research Unit

detail.title: On the impact of cross-ownership in a common property renewable resource oligopoly
detail.abstract: We construct a Markov Perfect Nash Equilibrium of a dynamic Cournot oligopoly where firms jointly exploit a productive asset (renewable resource) and engage in rival cross-shareholdings. We show that there exists an interval of stocks where cross-ownership can (i) increase market output, (ii) be profitable, and (iii) increase social welfare, both in the short run and at the steady state. These effects are in stark contrast with those obtained in a static oligopoly framework with strategic substitutes.

title: Technological Change and Racial Wage Gaps
