detail.title: Technological Change and Racial Wage Gaps

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Cleveland Working Paper No. 26-09
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The wage gap between Black and white Americans narrowed in the 1960s-1970s but stagnated after 1980. This study argues that routine-biased technological change (RBTC) contributed to this stagnation by affecting Black and white male workers differently across the wage distribution. Using new empirical evidence on occupational patterns and wage determinants for these workers, I rationalize these patterns with a novel RBTC theoretical framework. Contrary to expectations, Black workers' employment in routine-intensive occupations increased, while white workers experienced a significant decline. Applying the Oaxaca-RIF decomposition, I show that occupational sorting amplifies wage gaps, particularly at the lower end of the wage distribution. These findings, interpreted through the novel theoretical framework, offer new insights into the mechanisms driving racial wage gaps at the close of the twentieth century.

title: Mismeasuring Volatility Risk: Cross-Sectional Dispersion and the Distortion of Black-Scholes

detail.title: Mismeasuring Volatility Risk: Cross-Sectional Dispersion and the Distortion of Black-Scholes
detail.abstract: The standard deviation of implied volatility across option strikes, widely used by traders and central banks to measure volatility uncertainty, systematically overstates true dispersion due to three systematic biases. This paper contributes to the literature on market microstructure and volatility modeling by providing the first analytical decomposition of observed implied volatility dispersion. While previous studies (Hentschel, 2003; Bakshi & Kapadia, 2003) have identified individual biases, this framework integrates extraction error, jump-risk, and temporal aggregation into a single, bias-corrected metric: the True Volatility Dispersion Index (TVDI). Beyond theoretical refinement, we demonstrate the economic significance of this bias: during crisis periods, the use of conventional dispersion metrics leads to a systematic overestimation of regulatory capital requirements in notional exposure. This suggests that current Basel III-aligned risk frameworks may inadvertently mandate inefficient capital buffers due to measurement error.

title: State, Banking, and Industrial Productivity: The Chinese Financial System in Historical-Institutional Perspective
affiliations: Centro Universitário das Américas

detail.title: State, Banking, and Industrial Productivity: The Chinese Financial System in Historical-Institutional Perspective
detail.abstract: This article examines the Chinese financial system as an institutional arrangement in which finance operates in alignment with industrial productivity. Drawing on the theoretical foundations of Friedrich List and Gustav Schmoller, the study revisits the German Historical School to interpret contemporary financial development in China. While China hosts one of the largest capital market systems in the world, the article argues that the defining feature of its financial architecture lies in the structural role of the banking sector. Large-scale credit allocation toward manufacturing, infrastructure, and strategic industries suggests that financial institutions function as instruments of long-term capability accumulation and technological upgrading. The findings challenge the assumption that financial liberalization and autonomous capital markets are necessary conditions for industrial growth. Instead, the Chinese case illustrates how finance, when embedded within coordinated institutional structures, can serve as a complementary mechanism supporting productive development.

title: The O-5 Architecture: A Structural Answer to Executive Short-Termism

detail.title: The O-5 Architecture: A Structural Answer to Executive Short-Termism
detail.abstract: The four-year gubernatorial election cycle inherently optimizes for legibility over structural stability, creating a continuous cycle of destruction and reinvention that constitutes systemic waste. This paper proposes the O-5 Architecture, a constraint mechanism designed to prevent the executive branch from destroying state value through preventable short-termism. By establishing an architectural and oversight body operating on a staggered 2.1-year offset from the governor's term, funded completely by non-discretionary legislative mandate, the state forces the executive branch to design, execute, and be measured against long-term structural solutions. The O-5 Council engineers long-term systemic stability using democratic accountability rather than authoritarian mandate. By utilizing a public data ledger, mandatory anti-externalization audits, and enforcing a fiduciary duty to the long-term structural stability of the state, this framework replaces destructive political gridlock with constructive, measurable friction.

title: The Overconfidence Paradox: Reservation Returns and Investor Beliefs
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Overconfidence Paradox: Reservation Returns and Investor Beliefs
detail.abstract: Reservation return, the minimum acceptable return required to invest in the stock market, is fundamental yet understudied in finance. Much like reservation wages explain unemployment, reservation returns explain limited stock market participation, with important implications for household financial decisions. We develop a theoretical framework linking reservation return to overconfidence and derive an inverse relationship under mean-variance utility. Taking this to the data, however, we find a positive and statistically significant relationship, constituting the overconfidence paradox. We reconcile this by conjecturing that overconfident investors inflate expected returns while simultaneously raising perceived risk and aspiration benchmarks, rather than compressing volatility. To address endogeneity, we employ an IV strategy using experience-weighted market return moments as instruments. The IV results confirm and amplify the positive relationship, with economic significance reaching 88% to 116% of the mean reservation return, establishing overconfidence as a first-order causal determinant of investor hurdle rates.

title: Affirmative Action for Men on the Economic Margins
affiliations: Lewis & Clark College - Lewis & Clark Law School

detail.title: Affirmative Action for Men on the Economic Margins
detail.abstract: Male workers are falling behind.  Whether measured by earnings, labor-force participation, or educational outcomes, men have experienced steep declines over the last several decades.  Global competition and deindustrialization have gutted male-dominated fields.  Until men at the bottom of the labor market adjust their job-seeking behaviors to these larger economic forces, they will continue to experience lower earnings, higher unemployment rates, and the negative social costs that come with these dynamics.  Whereas more women have entered formerly male-dominated industries (e.g., management, law, and medicine), the “feminizing” of these sectors has not coincided with the “masculinizing” of lower-paid sectors where female workers predominate (e.g., teaching, nursing, and care work).  The underrepresentation of men in paid caregiving generates distinct harms for men and women.  Lower-skilled male workers avoid care work, despite abundant job openings.  At the same time, the dearth of men in this sector reinforces the occupational feminization of care work and the cultural assumption that only women perform this type of labor.  To bridge this divide, the Article asserts that employers in caregiving fields should enact workplace affirmative action plans that explicitly recruit and preference men.  The Supreme Court has approved of hiring preferences that counteract significant workplace gender imbalances.  The Article explains how preferring male workers in caregiving fields would satisfy the Court’s test for gender-based affirmative action, while simultaneously combatting systems of sex segregation that hamper employment opportunities for all workers.  Making the case for a new form of affirmative action, the Article marks the first scholarly attempt to extend hiring preferences to economically vulnerable men.

title: Aid Shocks and Political Conflict: Evidence from the Disruption to United States Foreign Aid
affiliations: New York University (NYU)

detail.title: Aid Shocks and Political Conflict: Evidence from the Disruption to United States Foreign Aid
detail.abstract: How do foreign aid shocks affect political conflict? I answer this question by (1) leveraging the exogenously timed disruption to United States foreign assistance in 2025, (2) building a novel dataset of subnational locations of foreign assistance projects, and (3) conducting a pre-registered analysis. I find that the disruption caused a substantial increase in conflict, including conflict that is typically driven by armed groups (such as battles) as well as conflict typically driven by civilians (such as riots). I provide evidence for the most likely mechanisms for each type of actor. To explain the increase in conflicts involving armed groups, I propose a theory in which the abrupt loss of aid signals short-term state weakness, which creates incentives for rebels to attack while they are in a relative state of power. The paper expands the evidence-base and theory for how aid impacts conflict, with important implications for policy.

detail.abstract:
Most systematic equity backtests operate under a silent assumption: that capital is fully invested at all times. This assumption is computationally convenient but structurally inconsistent with how professional capital actually behaves. Real strategies hold cash, wait for signals, and treat inactivity as a valid outcome.

This paper examines capital deployment efficiency as a measurable and meaningful attribute of systematic strategy design. Using a 17-year empirical study of the Phoenix Equity Timing Strategy (PETS) across 567 symbols from 2008 to 2025, we observe that the strategy maintained an average capital deployment of approximately 79% over the full period. Rather than representing idle inefficiency, this deployment profile reflects the architecture of an opportunity-driven system that deploys capital when conditions are favorable and preserves optionality when they are not.

We argue that deployment efficiency, not signal accuracy alone, is a primary differentiator between strategies that compound well and those that merely perform well in backtests. The implications for institutional allocators and backtest design are discussed

detail.abstract: How does fiscal stimulus affect durable goods sales and to what extent does stimulus drive inflation? We study this question in the context of how the unprecedented pandemic fiscal stimulus affected household car purchases and auto prices. Using administrative data on vehicle registrations, we exploit the timing of nearly $900 billion in stimulus payments and geographic differences in program exposure to identify causal effects on sales. We find the stimulus increased purchases by 5.5 million vehicles (3.2%) during 2020-2022, implying a medium-run (3-year) marginal propensity to spend (MPX) on autos of 0.19 and a total marginal propensity to consume (MPC) of 0.47. Despite this substantial demand response, fiscal transfers account for less than 20% of the surge in auto prices. In a general equilibrium model with new and used markets, we show how secondary-market interactions dampen inflation. When transfers push households onto the new-car margin, trade-ins expand used supply and limit price increases. This channel weakens when supply is tight or when policy targets borrowing constraints, constraints, relaxed credit conditions, and preference shifts, explain the majority of the observed inflation. in which case stimulus manifests more as inflation than output. detail.title: Predictably Unpredictable Inspections

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-43

detail.abstract: Inspections are a common tool for acquiring information and incentivizing compliance. Although inspections are typically unannounced, their timing often follows a predictable schedule. We study how this predictability shapes firm effort and patient outcomes in U.S. nursing homes, leveraging detailed administrative data on staffing, care, and health outcomes. Nursing homes "slack" in the low-risk period following an inspection and ramp up effort as their next inspection approaches. Patient survival mirrors this pattern, suggesting that these fluctuations in effort have meaningful consequences for the quality of patient care. We embed these estimates in a dynamic model capturing how inspection regimes incentivize effort and provide information about quality. Our estimates indicate that moving to unpredictable inspections could induce as much additional effort as increasing the frequency of inspections by 12%, while only minimally reducing their informational value.

title: From IoT to AIoT: Cybersecurity and Legal Governance of Autonomous Infrastructure Systems

detail.title: From IoT to AIoT: Cybersecurity and Legal Governance of Autonomous Infrastructure Systems

publicationDetails.detailsText: Raj, Mukund (2026). From IoT to AIoT: Cybersecurity and Legal Governance of Autonomous Infrastructure Systems.

detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has transformed modern infrastructure systems by embedding connectivity, sensors, and data analytics into physical environments. More recently, the integration of artificial intelligence into IoT ecosystems has given rise to Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT), enabling autonomous decision-making within cyber-physical infrastructure systems. While these developments offer significant operational efficiencies, they also introduce new cybersecurity risks, governance challenges, and legal complexities. 

This paper examines the evolution from IoT to AIoT and analyzes emerging cybersecurity threats associated with connected infrastructure systems. It further evaluates the adequacy of existing regulatory frameworks and proposes a governance-oriented policy framework to strengthen accountability, resilience, and security in AI-driven infrastructure environments. 

By examining applications across smart cities, transportation systems, consumer IoT devices, and digital twins, the paper highlights the growing importance of cybersecurity governance in the emerging era of autonomous infrastructure systems.

detail.abstract: Global financial systems are approaching a significant paradigm shift, catalyzed by accelerated research and development efforts on Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC). The current correspondent banking model for cross-border payments harbors persistent inefficiencies, including high transaction costs, slow settlement times (typically T+2), and operational opacity [1], [2]. Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) presents a revolutionary solution to these frictions by providing a common infrastructure that enables secure, automated, and near-instantaneous value transfers [3]. This report seeks to demonstrate that global monetary authorities have made CBDC development a priority to remedy long-standing inefficiencies. As of the first quarter of 2025, 134 countries, representing 98% of the Global GDP, are actively engaged in CBDC initiatives. Notably, all G20 members are participating, and 13 of them (including Brazil, Japan, India, and Türkiye) have entered the advanced pilot phase [4]. Pioneering international collaborations define the technical and operational contours of this emerging architecture. The mBridge project, which has reached the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) stage, has convened the central banks of China, Hong Kong, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, and Saudi Arabia on a single platform to promote local currency payments.

affiliations: Kansai University and Tokyo University of Science

detail.title: Preference-Free Asset Pricing: Additive Separation of Risk and Ambiguity
detail.abstract: This paper derives a tractable multi-asset pricing formula separating risk and ambiguity within a robust control framework. Unlike existing multiplicative models, our terminal wealth maximization approach-using a general utility function-yields a strikingly simple additive decomposition of the pricing kernel. We demonstrate that the total asset premium is the linear sum of a traditional risk premium and a distinct ambiguity premium. Crucially, the equilibrium relationship remains structurally identical to the classical CAPM. This result is preference-free, being invariant to risk and ambiguity aversion, providing a practical, ambiguity-inclusive pricing formula independent of unobservable subjective parameters.

detail.abstract: Marine tourism represents a strategic sector in the economic development of coastal regions, particularly in archipelagic countries such as Indonesia. Raja Ampat is internationally recognized as a premier marine tourism destination with exceptional biodiversity. This paper examines the impact of tourism on local community income in Raja Ampat and identifies key lessons learned from its development. Using a qualitative literature review approach, this study synthesizes findings from academic research on marine tourism economics and community-based management. The analysis shows that tourism contributes to increased local income through employment generation, livelihood diversification, and significant multiplier effects. However, tourism-derived income is volatile and highly dependent on tourist arrivals and environmental quality. The paper highlights the importance of community participation and sustainable resource management to ensure long-term and equitable economic benefits.

title: Stock Market Volatility: Shiller Test and Developments

detail.title: Stock Market Volatility: Shiller Test and Developments
detail.abstract: This paper investigates stock market volatility through an econometric extension of Shiller’s variance bounds test over the period 1871–2024. Using monthly S&P 500 data, I compare actual prices with fundamentals-based ex-post prices and show that actual stock prices are about twice as volatile as justified by dividends and discount rates, confirming a persistent rejection of the Efficient Market Hypothesis. I then quantify the role of macroeconomic policy and speculative activity in explaining this excess volatility. Counterfactual simulations for 2001–2024 indicate that expansionary monetary policy reduces conditional equity volatility by approximately 42% during major crisis episodes. Rolling-window Granger causality tests on 9,143 daily observation windows reveal that speculative trading Granger-causes volatility in 62.17% of cases, whereas reverse causality from volatility to speculation appears in only 0.77% of windows, with the remainder characterized by bidirectional or insignificant relationships. Finally, I propose an alternative valuation framework that integrates neoclassical present-value pricing with a class-based perspective, documenting a strong empirical correlation between the declining labor income share and rising price-to-dividend ratios over 1980–2024. Taken together, the results suggest that excess volatility is structurally linked to speculative dynamics, monetary policy interventions, and distributional shifts rather than to fundamentals alone.

title: XAI-Enhancer: Hierarchical feature aggregation for highly faithful model explanations in gastrointestinal image classification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, IIT Guwahati and University of Eastern Finland

detail.title: XAI-Enhancer: Hierarchical feature aggregation for highly faithful model explanations in gastrointestinal image classification
detail.abstract: Background and ObjectiveDeep learning, augmented by Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), shows substantial potential in medical imaging. However, traditional Class Activation Mapping (CAM) methods often rely solely on final convolutional layers, limiting their efficacy in capturing the holistic, textural anomalies typical of medical conditions. This reliance compromises explanation faithfulness, hindering accurate clinical decision-making. To mitigate this, we propose XAI-Enhancer, a novel methodology that integrates spatial information from all convolutional layers of a deep learning model.MethodsBy linearly combining layer-specific explanations weighted by logit similarity derived from masked activations, XAIEnhancer generates superior explanation maps. Rigorous experimentation across five standard architectures (VGG and ResNet families) on two diverse gastrointestinal datasets: the Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) dataset and the multi-class Kvasir-v2 dataset, demonstrates the robustness and generalizability of the proposed method.ResultsQuantitative evaluations reveal that XAI-Enhancer consistently outperforms existing single-layer CAM methods and multilayer aggregation techniques (e.g., LayerCAM, HR-CAM) across Deletion, Insertion, and the Remove And Debias (ROAD) metrics. Crucially, this layer-wise evaluation exposes severe, dataset-dependent structural bottlenecks in residual networks, demonstrating that spatial degradation is erratic and highly unpredictable rather than uniformly correlated with architectural depth.ConclusionsBy dynamically compensating for these bottlenecks and effectively balancing high-frequency textural variations with deep semantic features, the XAI-Enhancer produces highly faithful explanations, thereby advancing the trustworthiness of AI-assisted medical diagnostics.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the determinants of economic competitiveness in Argentina during the 2004–2025 period. The local debate often attributes the productive sector's difficulties to episodes of exchange rate appreciation. However, the evidence presented here suggests that the main problem lies in the stagnation of productivity. Based on data from the Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA), INDEC, and the OECD, it is shown that the level of the real exchange rate is within normal historical ranges, while productivity has shown a sustained negative trend since 2008. Chronic macroeconomic volatility and a low investment rate—consistently below 18% of GDP—constitute structural constraints that explain the loss of competitiveness more than the exchange rate level itself. It is concluded that policies focused exclusively on the exchange rate have only transitory effects if not accompanied by a productivity agenda based on macroeconomic stability and long-term investment.

title: Is Great Britian Better Off Since Brexit?

detail.title: Is Great Britian Better Off Since Brexit?
detail.abstract: In this paper, I primarily focus on three time periods.  The first time period from 1945 to 1993 was before EU participation.  The second time period is from 1993 to 2020.  The third time period is from 2021- 2025, the years following EU membership.  How does it affect the trajectory of the nation? What effect did joining the EU have on the economy at large? In the following sections, consideration will be taken for economic and political factors that are used to assess the question “Is Great Britain better off in the years since Brexit?”  The results found that the prosperity of Great Britain decreased immediately, mainly because of Co-vid 19, and it regained its prior levels with the EU-UK Cooperative agreement that was signed in 2021. Great Britain can continue to be prosperous without membership to the European Union.

title: A Total Variation Regularized and Inverse Probability Weighted Accelerated Failure Time Model for Scalar-on-Image Regression with Right-Censored Data
affiliations: Changchun University of Technology, Changchun University of Technology, Changchun University of Technology and Changchun University of Technology

detail.title: A Total Variation Regularized and Inverse Probability Weighted Accelerated Failure Time Model for Scalar-on-Image Regression with Right-Censored Data
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: With the rapid advancement of medical and imaging technologies, multi-modal imaging techniques such as MRI, fMRI, DTI, and PET have become increasingly important in clinical diagnosis and cohort studies. In clinical research, the timing of event occurrences is often of primary interest. However, survival time data is frequently right-censored due to factors like follow-up termination or loss to follow-up. Medical imaging data contains rich spatial structural information and exhibits extremely high dimensionality. In the context of right-censored data, we incorporate medical imaging as high-dimensional covariates within the Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) modeling framework to explore the impact of imaging features on survival time.    Methods:We propose a  regression framework for high-dimensional imaging data with right-censored outcomes by combining a weighted objective function with Total Variation (TV) regularization. The weighting scheme accounts for the censored data structure, while the TV penalty captures the spatial continuity and boundary features of imaging effects, improving model interpretability and the identification of important regions.   Results: Across a range of sample sizes and censoring rates, the TV-regularized approach consistently outperformed Matrix-Reg and Lasso in recovering spatially structured imaging effects. TV produced more stable estimates and better preserved key signal features (especially boundaries and change points), whereas Lasso tended to over-shrink and yield fragmented local patterns. Matrix-Reg showed intermediate performance, improving with larger sample sizes and lower censoring, but becoming blurrier and losing fine-scale details as censoring increased. Overall, the TV-regularized method demonstrated the best robustness and adaptability under right-censoring.   Conclusion:The TV regularization method exhibits more continuous, connected block effects. It forms more concentrated and stronger positive/negative effect clusters in a few localized regions, consistent with the prior assumption that imaging effects are spatially continuous and clustered. This approach is also beneficial for subsequent brain region template mapping, stability evaluation, and cross-method overlap analysis, thereby enhancing medical interpretability.

title: The Hidden Plumbing of Stablecoins: Financial and Technological Risks in the GENIUS Act Era
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), , , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - MIT Media Laboratory and

detail.title: The Hidden Plumbing of Stablecoins: Financial and Technological Risks in the GENIUS Act Era
detail.abstract: U.S. dollar stablecoins are increasingly used as payment and settlement instruments beyond cryptocurrency markets. With the enactment of the GENIUS Act in 2025, the United States established the first comprehensive federal framework governing their issuance, backing, and supervision. This paper evaluates the financial, technological, and regulatory risks that may arise as GENIUS-compliant stablecoins scale into mainstream use. We show that maintaining par-value redemption may depend not only on backing-asset quality, but also on the functioning of Treasury and repo markets, the balance-sheet capacity of broker-dealers, and the operational reliability of blockchain-based transaction rails. Even conservatively backed stablecoins can face stress from redemption surges, market-intermediation bottlenecks, or technological disruptions. We argue that durable stability will likely require an integrated approach spanning financial-market infrastructure, prudential regulation, and software governance. While grounded in U.S. law, the analysis identifies principles that are relevant for regulators in other jurisdictions developing stablecoin regimes.

title: Signals from SMS: Alternative Data and Distributional Effects in Credit Scoring
affiliations: Northwestern University,  and AFINIT

detail.title: Signals from SMS: Alternative Data and Distributional Effects in Credit Scoring
detail.abstract: Using data from 23 million loan applications from a FinTech lender in India, we demonstrate how transaction records and credit histories can be extracted from text messages and used to assess applicants' creditworthiness. We show that an alternative credit scoring system built on these data and machine-learning algorithms predicts consumer delinquency more accurately than traditional credit scores, with gains attributable to both algorithmic improvements and the use of alternative data. We find that this alternative credit scoring system expands credit access by approving loans to new-to-credit applicants with no credit bureau score. However, the benefits of this technological shift are skewed toward financially advantaged groups, due to differences in the amount of extractable information rather than due to algorithmic bias. Requesting additional information does not fully address this disparity: financially disadvantaged groups are less willing to share their data, and even when they provide their data, the additional datasets exhibit uneven coverage of financially informative signals. Our results suggest that underwriting systems need to address frictions in both data-sharing willingness and unequal availability of financial information to achieve truly inclusive credit assessment.

title: Within-Task Competence Heterogeneity and the Shape of Technological Displacement: A Generalization of Task-Based Automation Models

detail.title: Within-Task Competence Heterogeneity and the Shape of Technological Displacement: A Generalization of Task-Based Automation Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Acemoglu and Restrepo's task-based framework models automation as a threshold sweeping across a continuum of tasks, producing monotonic decline in labor's share. We show that this monotonic displacement result arises as the κ → 0 limiting case of a more general model in which automation thresholds sweep across distributions of human competence within tasks. We relax this assumption by modeling human competence on each task as a truncated normal distribution governed by a single parameter, κ = (s max-µ)/σ, which measures within-task performance heterogeneity. We prove that κ → 0 recovers the Acemoglu-Restrepo step function as a limiting case (Proposition 1), while large κ produces a spike-cliff trajectory in which per-expert value grows superexponentially before collapsing discontinuously (Proposition 2). When a professional performs tasks with heterogeneous κ values, aggregate displacement is nonmonotonic (Proposition 3, the Hump Theorem): early automation reduces value, late automation produces a spike, and the resolution is a cliff. We extend the framework to domains where AI errors carry catastrophic consequences, formalizing conditions for asymptotic black swan fragility. We then endogenize AI capability and expert supply, proving that the private equilibrium enters the gamma gap (AI beyond human oversight capacity) strictly before the socially optimal path, because firms internalize automation profits but not the option value of preserving oversight capacity. The welfare wedge is largest during the spike, when the market signal suggests experts are thriving. An illustrative calibration using software engineering data demonstrates the quantitative plausibility of the spike-cliff trajectory.

title: GenAI for All? Unequal Impacts on Women in STEM Entrepreneurship
affiliations: Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California, Mays Business School, Texas A&M University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: GenAI for All? Unequal Impacts on Women in STEM Entrepreneurship
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified debate over whether new digital technologies democratize economic participation or instead exacerbate inequality. We study this question in the context of STEM entrepreneurship, where both gender disparities and the relevance of GenAI are especially pronounced. Leveraging the public release of ChatGPT as a quasi-exogenous expansion in access to GenAI capabilities, we examine how GenAI reshapes gender inequality at the point of entrepreneurial entry rather than among incumbent entrepreneurs. Using U.S. Current Population Survey data, we find that GenAI access is associated with higher rates of incorporated STEM entrepreneurship overall, but has no average effect on the gender gap. This null aggregate effect, however, masks substantial geographic heterogeneity. In economically stronger regions, GenAI access narrows the gender gap in STEM entrepreneurial entry, whereas it widens the gap in economically weaker regions. These findings reveal a digital outcome divide: even when frontier AI technologies become broadly accessible, their participation benefits are unevenly realized across locations. Overall, our results show that GenAI is general-purpose in capability but conditional in inclusiveness. We thus highlight entrepreneurial participation as a critical and underexamined margin through which generative AI reshapes gender inequality.

title: Systemic Risk Assessment of Geopolitical Energy Shocks: A Macroprudential Stress-Test Framework for Strait of Hormuz Disruption and Cross-Border Transmission to Sovereign Debt Markets
affiliations: University of Buckingham

detail.title: Systemic Risk Assessment of Geopolitical Energy Shocks: A Macroprudential Stress-Test Framework for Strait of Hormuz Disruption and Cross-Border Transmission to Sovereign Debt Markets
detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive stress-test analysis of sustained geopolitical conflict involving Iran, Israel, and the United States, with particular emphasis on disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz the world's most critical oil chokepoint handling approximately 20% of global petroleum consumption (U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2025). Using a Global Vector Autoregression (GVAR) framework informed by Chudik and Pesaran (2015) and structural shock identification methodologies from Baumeister and Hamilton (2019), we model four scenarios ranging from baseline stability to extreme 90% supply disruption. Our findings indicate that an extreme scenario would generate oil price shocks of 220% ($78 to $250 per barrel), triggering catastrophic macroeconomic consequences for import-dependent emerging markets. For Ghana, the analysis projects inflation accelerating to 62%, currency depreciation of 85%, and GDP contraction of 4.2%, with fuel import bills surging from $3.2 billion to $14.2 billion annually. The transmission mechanism operates through multiple channels including supply-side cost shocks (Rotemberg and Woodford, 1996), exchange rate pass-through (Taylor, 2000; Ca' Zorzi, Hahn and Sanchez, 2007), and sovereign risk premium explosions (Alturki and Hibbert, 2021). We identify crisis-alpha investment opportunities in gold, crude oil futures, and defense equities, while recommending immediate policy interventions including monetary tightening, fiscal consolidation, and strategic reserve management. This research contributes to the literature on energy-inflation pass-through in developing economies (De Gregorio, 2012; Auer et al., 2024) and provides actionable intelligence for risk management in an era of heightened geopolitical volatility.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates the impact of Islamic banking windows on lending behavior and credit risk in Tanzanian commercial banks, utilizing panel data from 25 banks over the period 2018-2024. Following the pioneering entry of Islamic windows by major conventional banks in 2021 and the subsequent Banking and Financial Institutions (Non-Interest Banking Business) Regulations, 2025, this research employs Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS), System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM), and Pooled Mean Group (PMG) estimation to examine the relationships between window adoption, lending volume, and credit risk. The findings reveal that Islamic window adoption significantly increases lending volume by approximately 28.4%, demonstrating that windows expand overall credit supply rather than merely substituting conventional lending. However, banks operating Islamic windows exhibit significantly higher credit risk, with non-performing loan ratios approximately 0.62 percentage points above banks without windows, and larger window operations are associated with elevated parent bank risk. Crucially, capital adequacy moderates this relationship, with the marginal effect of window adoption declining substantially at higher capital levels, highlighting the protective role of capital buffers. Sectoral analysis indicates that banks with windows maintain more concentrated lending portfolios, with higher exposure to trade, agriculture, and real estate—sectors amenable to Islamic financing modes such as Murabahah and Ijarah. Dynamic panel analysis confirms strong persistence in both lending and credit risk, with windows showing slower adjustment to risk deviations. The study concludes that while Islamic windows enhance financial inclusion and credit access, they introduce elevated credit risk that requires robust capital buffers, specialized risk management frameworks, and vigilant regulatory oversight. These findings inform the implementation of the 2025 Regulations and provide evidence-based guidance for bank managers, regulators, and policymakers in developing sustainable Islamic banking in Tanzania's dual banking system.

title: Mapping the Future of Labor Rights Enforcement in Global Value Chains: A Comparative Analysis of Labor Governance Approaches
affiliations: , Tel Aviv University - Buchmann Faculty of Law and Tel Aviv University - Buchmann Faculty of Law

Views and opinions expressed are however those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or European Research Council Executive Agency (ERCEA) (the ‘granting authority’). detail.abstract:
The quest for effective enforcement of labor rights in global value chains lies at the intersection of innovation and expectation, requiring both a reimagining of non-enforceable and legally binding instruments, and a critical examination of emerging institutions that promise change even in the absence of traditional enforcement mechanisms. On one hand, it is essential to assess non-enforceable instruments (both de jure and de facto) and consider whether socio-economic incentives for compliance can substitute for "hard" legal enforcement. On the other hand, it is crucial to refine our understanding of how to develop effective enforcement measures by critically examining whether emerging institutions oriented toward this goal can fulfill their promise.

In this twofold inquiry, this article places greater emphasis on the second question while still giving necessary attention to the first. By mapping several potential pathways for the enforcement of workers’ rights in GVCs, we argue that strict adherence to a simple link between norms and enforcement mechanisms fails to address the range of challenges encountered on the ground. Seeking both to analytically understand and to reframe enforcement in light of the complex, transnational, and multi-tiered realities of GVCs, we draw on existing institutional developments already embedded within the transnational governance system, whether routinely applied or still under development.

title: The Rational Cover-Up
affiliations: Universidad de los Andes, Chile - ESE Business School

detail.title: The Rational Cover-Up

The author has previously provided advisory services to mining companies and corporate boards in Latin America in an independent capacity. detail.abstract:
Six workers dead. Thirty-one months of falsified and incomplete technical data submitted to the regulator. Entire mine sectors operating without permits deleted from official filings. The information system that should have protected workers was compromised across the entire mine, not only in isolated zones. And a distributed benefit of US$830 to US$920 million among all stakeholders—including the very State that was supposed to oversee.

What happened at Codelco's El Teniente mine, the world's largest underground copper operation, is not the story of a handful of dishonest executives. It is the anatomy of a governance architecture that made the cover-up the economically rational decision at every level of the organization. This essay identifies four conditions whose simultaneous interaction produces what I call a governance architecture of predictable disaster: existential pressure for production, corruption of information channels, a board without sufficient technical oversight capacity, and a structurally dependent regulator. None is sufficient on its own; it is their simultaneous configuration that eliminates every line of defense. Through forensic analysis of the case and its comparison with five major international disasters—BP, Vale, Pike River, Boeing, and Massey Energy—the essay demonstrates that the pattern is transferable across industries and jurisdictions. The analysis integrates for the first time the distinction between personal safety and process safety into the corporate governance framework, and identifies a causal mechanism specific to state-owned enterprises in high-hazard industries: from fiscal extraction to incentive misalignment, to information corruption, to physical harm. The essay does not question Codelco's state ownership. What it questions is a governance architecture that proved incompatible with the safety of the people who work in it.

title: Endogenous Payroll Tax Wedge and Labor Spatial Misallocation
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University

detail.title: Endogenous Payroll Tax Wedge and Labor Spatial Misallocation
detail.abstract: Spatial misallocation of labor, driven by institutional frictions that inhibit factor agglomeration in high-productivity cities, is a key constraint on aggregate efficiency in developing countries. This paper studies a previously underexplored source of endogenous spatial friction: the localized design of China's social insurance system, where mandatory contribution floors and ceilings are indexed to localized average wages. We show that this design creates a novel self-reinforcing feedback loop: localized payroll tax wedges distort migration and spatial sorting of heterogeneous workers, which in turn reshapes local wage distributions and the magnitude of the wedges themselves. We structurally estimate a quantitative spatial general equilibrium model using 2017 China Migrants Dynamic Survey (CMDS) microdata and a hand-collected dataset of city-level social insurance policies. Our counterfactual analysis yields three core findings. First, these endogenous wedges significantly reduce labor agglomeration in high-productivity urban hubs, acting as a regressive entry tax on low-skilled workers. Second, full elimination of the contribution floors raises aggregate output by 1.73%, with welfare gains concentrated among low-skilled workers (3.93%). Third, unifying the contribution indexing benchmark at the provincial level increases aggregate output by 3.74%, with balanced welfare improvements across skill groups. Our results highlight that reforming the localized design of social insurance systems can deliver substantial gains in both aggregate efficiency and equity.

title: Managing Resources against Illiquidity and Sustainable Banking Business
affiliations: Rhema Univeristy, Nigeria.

detail.title: Managing Resources against Illiquidity and Sustainable Banking Business
detail.abstract: Managing resources is central to organizational sustainability, especially in the delicate areas of banking business. This is critical because banks act as payment agents by conducting deposit and current accounts for customers, paying cheques drawn by customers on the bank and collecting cheques deposited to customers' current accounts. Banks also facilitate customer payments through other payment methods such as mail transfers and others. In these banking processes, liquidity is of great importance. Liquidity is a measure that a bank is in a position to keep pace with its liabilities as they mature for payment. On the other hands, a bank is said to have liquidity problems when the value of its realizable assets is less than the total value of its liabilities, and thus a position of illiquidity. This is what exactly played out in the 1990s when the average liquidity ratio dropped from 0.49 percent before 1995 to minus 15.92 percent in December, 1995, exposing a severe situation of illiquidity, distress and consequent bank failures in Nigeria. The exploratory qualitative research design was adopted for the study and the result showed significant positive relationship between managing resources and sustainable banking business. This study was not exhaustive due to lack of current relevant literature and research funding. Further research could examine the relationship between business plan and bank liquidity in Nigeria. The study recommends for proper corporate strategy to serve as a key driver of sustainable banking business.

title: The Impact of the Russian-Ukrainian Conflict on World Grain Markets
affiliations: The University of Western Australia

detail.title: The Impact of the Russian-Ukrainian Conflict on World Grain Markets
detail.abstract:
In response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine on 24th February 2022, grain shipments through the Black Sea were suspended, causing a sharp rise in grain prices. A UN sanctioned deal, the Black Sea Grain Initiative, allowed trade in food and fertiliser to continue from August 2022. However, that deal was suspended in July 2023, once again putting at risk food security in those countries dependent on grain imports. 
As the protracted conflict continues, it remains to be seen what the longer-term impacts might be. We use a global CGE model to assess the trade impacts of the production shortfall in Ukraine plus the Black Sea blockade. We show that with time to adjust, the medium-term price impacts are relatively modest but the quantity impacts are more significant. Developing country importers are affected more by shortages of coarse grains than wheat or oilseeds. Implications for Australian and other grain exporters are estimated. The role of open international markets is critical to subdue food security concerns. This means that export restrictions need to be kept to a minimum if prices are to be kept down.

title: The Sovereign Imperative
affiliations: Cybersecurity Advisor & Implementor

detail.title: The Sovereign Imperative
detail.abstract: India stands at a strategic paradox. With a GDP approaching $4 trillion, the world's fastest-growing major developer community (21.9 million GitHub accounts, surpassing the United States in opensource contributions), and a celebrated Digital India ecosystem, the nation projects an image of sovereign technological prowess. Beneath that surface, however, lies a systemic and dangerous dependency on foreign-controlled infrastructure across every critical layer of the digital stack. The threat is no longer theoretical. In July 2025, Microsoft unilaterally suspended data and software services to Nayara Energy-an Indian oil refinery processing 20 million tonnes of crude annually-to comply with European Union sanctions targeting Russian stakeholders. No Indian court ordered it; no Indian law required it. A foreign corporation made a compliance decision that threatened the operational continuity of critical national energy infrastructure. This was not a cyberattack. It was a corporate kill switch, and India had no override. This paper systematically maps India's foundational technology dependencies across ten critical domains-cloud computing, enterprise software, developer toolchains, telecommunications, industrial control systems (SCADA), engineering R&D tools, semiconductors, medical devices, internet governance, and financial routing. Each domain represents a potential point of forced paralysis in the event of a geopolitical crisis, trade sanction, or targeted corporate blockade.

title: The Redistributive Effects of Sectoral Shocks
affiliations: and London School of Economics

detail.title: The Redistributive Effects of Sectoral Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the redistributive impacts of sectoral shocks. We develop a new model combining features from both the heterogeneous agents and input-output literature, which is amenable to analyse how idiosyncratic shocks propagation redistribute wealth and income within sectors. We find that key sectors in shock transmission can be identified using the sectoral influence centrality measure. Our model also suggests that negative supply shocks generate positive redistribution effects for the supplying sector, whereas receiving industries suffer distributional costs. We extend our analysis by introducing fiscal policies and show that while labor tax shocks trigger homogeneous responses for inequalities across sectors, capital tax shocks generate very heterogeneous responses with substantial distributional costs.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the limits of corporate governance as a tool for advancing climate transition. While capital market mechanisms, shareholder stewardship, say-on-climate votes, and ESG-linked executive compensation are often presented as effective levers for greening corporate behavior, their transformative capacity is systematically constrained. Building on insights from financial economics and agency theory, the paper highlights incentive distortions within the complex investment ecosystem and introduces the “waterbed effect” as a central, yet underappreciated, limitation. Firm-specific governance interventions alter marginal abatement incentives asymmetrically, inducing competitive reallocation of emissions or production that may fully offset intended environmental gains. A formal model demonstrates how such interventions fail to reduce aggregate emissions under emissions trading systems and may even be counterproductive in competitive product markets. The analysis suggests that corporate governance can complement, but not substitute for, universally applicable regulatory instruments such as carbon pricing or comprehensive emissions caps. Overreliance on governance-based solutions risks inefficient resource allocation and may crowd out the political momentum necessary for effective climate regulation.

title: Learning Lessons Across Borders

detail.title: Learning Lessons Across Borders
detail.abstract: This chapters provides the Introduction to the wider collection: C. Bevan (Ed.), The Routledge Handbook of Global Perspectives on Homelessness, Law & Policy (2024, Routledge). Homelessness is a global challenge that warrants a global perspective. Yet homelessness also presents a global opportunity-to learn lessons across borders and to innovate and inspire new thinking and novel ways of 'seeing' homelessness from a genuinely international perspective. This collection draws on the diverse, rich tapestry of experiences of homelessness and homelessness prevention across 28 different nations from each of the permanently inhabited continents and seeks to nourish and inform debates both at the state and international level as well as within global institutions on how best to respond to and tackle this most damaging global social phenomenon and human tragedy. While every nation on Earth has its own history and socio-political landscape, the fundamental need of citizens for secure and stable housing speaks in a universal language. This core human imperative for a safe place to call 'home' is shared by all populations and is one that sounds across history and transcends country lines. The United Nations estimates that over 1.6 billion people internationally are living in inadequate housing and over 100 million people have no housing whatsoever to call their own. Homelessness impacts every country and every community. In many parts of the world, homelessness is on the increase, fuelled by and coterminous with economic, social, and health inequalities. As this collection reveals, a broad range of powerful currents touches on homelessness, not least the tentacles of the Global Financial Crisis of 2008, which still echo in many nations of the world, but so, too, the Covid-19 pandemic, which has affected us all, but with varying degrees of severity. The pandemic both revealed but also perpetrated and exacerbated existing social global inequalities. Yet this book reveals, out of this most horrific human tragedy, that hopeful and forward-looking initiatives for homelessness prevention have sprouted. Homelessness is, as is well-known, a deeply complex problem which rests at the intersection of varied and connected social concerns. As well as housing precarity, therefore, this book demonstrates the interconnectedness of issues of housing, health, wealth, employment, politics, discrimination, and community and how these social determinants and drivers sit as enduring and dominant themes for homelessness research and for those living with homelessness. The chapters of this collection deftly map the relationship between these themes as they emerge and collide in each country studied.

title: The Macroprudential Response to Climate Systemic Risk: Four Essential Pillars

detail.title: The Macroprudential Response to Climate Systemic Risk: Four Essential Pillars

publicationDetails.detailsText: Council on Economic Policies Policy Briefs

detail.abstract:
Climate risks pose systemic risk, potentially undermining financial stability. Any systemic risk calls for an adequate macroprudential policy response, and climate systemic risk is no exception. Against this background, financial supervisors are assessing how to design effective macroprudential tools to address it.
While existing macroprudential policy toolkits can already be deployed to address climate-related systemic risk, their implementation shall account for the data available to assess climate-related risks, the state of knowledge about them, and the institutional frameworks in which macroprudential instruments operate. To be efficient, these measures must ensure that the financial system maintains its shock-absorbing capacity and that the buildup of financial vulnerabilities is contained.
This policy brief proposes four pillars to ground effective macroprudential instruments for addressing climate systemic risk. It highlights that such instruments should be grounded in forward-looking, dynamic approaches, entail incentives to mitigate the build-up of climate systemic risk, be integrated into comprehensive policy packages, and involve some degree of international coordination.

title: Uses of Macro Social Theory: A Social Housing Case Study

detail.title: Uses of Macro Social Theory: A Social Housing Case Study
detail.abstract: This article reflects on the use of macro social theoretical perspectives to explain micro social issues, using social housing allocations as a case study. In contrast to a number of social theoretical examinations of social housing allocation schemes in recent years, spanning socio-legal studies, we argue that 'cookie-cutter' theories may overlook other positions and counter-factual scenarios. We draw on a sample of local authority allocation schemes to reflect on the growing category of households (commonly termed 'unhouseables' by housing officers) which are excluded from appearing on such schemes because of their former housing deviance or some other disqualification. We offer a set of reflections grounded in our data, which focus on sustainability. Thus, rather than point to particular rationalities or the like, we offer particular housing issues as explanatory factors-including the declining stock and financial 'competitiveness' of social housing management-as well as a rise in punitiveness.

detail.abstract: Institutional corruption is commonly defined through observable violations such as bribery, abuse of office, or embezzlement. While such definitions capture measurable symptoms, they often fail to identify the structural mechanisms through which corruption becomes normalized across societies. This paper proposes a structural interpretation of corruption as a progressive misalignment between power, responsibility, and accountability. When institutional incentives reward misalignment over integrity, individuals gradually adapt to those incentives until corruption becomes embedded within everyday behavior. Drawing on field observations conducted between 2008 and 2015 within antiscorruption initiatives involving civil society organizations, parliamentary institutions, and international governance environments, this study examines how corruption extends beyond formal institutions into relational domains such as family structures, gender roles, and developmental environments. The analysis argues that gender disparity frequently emerges as an early diagnostic signal of institutional misalignment because relational systems absorb instability before political collapse becomes visible.

title: The Homelessness Reduction Act 2017: Furthering not Fracturing Marginalisation of those Experiencing Homelessness

detail.title: The Homelessness Reduction Act 2017: Furthering not Fracturing Marginalisation of those Experiencing Homelessness
detail.abstract: The Homelessness Reduction Act 2017 represents the most significant change to the rights of homeless people in England for decades. Through an analysis of the history of homelessness legislation in England, but focusing on the 'ground-breaking' 2017 Act, this article explores how the homeless population is represented and 'constructed' in this new legislation and what this tells us about the place of homeless people in our society. In so doing, this article exposes how the 2017 Act, a State instrument of apparent homelessness prevention, can be read and understood as contributing to rather than obviating the marginalisation and social exclusion of homeless people.

title: Augmenting Survey Data with Generative AI: An Application to Economic Research

detail.title: Augmenting Survey Data with Generative AI: An Application to Economic Research
detail.abstract: We study the potential of large language models (LLMs) to augment survey data collected from human subjects, by focusing on two applications: (1) estimating willingness-to-accept (WTA) for giving up digital and traditional goods, and (2) predicting personal income levels. We find that supplying LLMs with rich contextual data beyond demographics significantly improves predictive accuracy. Model fine tuning and retrieval augmented generation (RAG) further enhance performance, while changes to model temperature or prompting strategies yield only marginal improvements. Performance varies across goods studied and demographic groups. We provide a methodological blueprint for deploying LLMs as a fast, low cost multiplier of survey coverage. This is increasingly valuable given the rapid decline in survey response rates.

title: Exploring Legal Dimensions in Digital Linguistics
affiliations: KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP) and Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP), Faculty of Law - KU Leuven

detail.title: Exploring Legal Dimensions in Digital Linguistics

declarations.funderStatement: Leona King is funded by the Research Foundation – Flanders (FWO) [grant no. 11A0025N].

detail.abstract:
Digital linguistics increasingly relies on large-scale, heterogeneous language data drawn from online platforms, archives, and research infrastructures – data that may be personal, sensitive, creative, or subject to restrictions on access and reuse. Under EU data and digital legislation, however, “language data” is not recognised as a distinct legal category. Instead, linguistic research is shaped by a dense and evolving set of intersecting regulatory regimes that were not designed with linguistics in mind but nonetheless structure what researchers may collect, process, share, and publish. This chapter offers a structured, practice-oriented guide to the legal frameworks most relevant to digital linguistic research.

It explains how the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)’s broad notions of personal data and processing apply to common research workflows; how copyright and the sui generis database right affect corpus construction and redistribution; and how the text and data mining (TDM) exceptions introduced by the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive (CDSMD) aim to recalibrate lawful computational analysis. The chapter then situates language data within the EU’s newer data governance and platform regulation landscape, covering the Open Data Directive (ODD), the Data Governance Act (DGA), the Data Act (DA), and the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and Digital Services Act (DSA), and discusses the emerging role of Common European Data Spaces, particularly the European Language Data Space. Finally, it outlines how the AI Act’s data governance and transparency requirements may affect language technologies and linguistic datasets. The chapter concludes by synthesising cross-regime themes and identifying scenarios in which legal consultation may be advisable for researchers.

title: Fracture behavior and fracture parameter evaluation of notched specimens made from basalt fiber /glass fiber hybrid composite laminates

detail.title: Fracture behavior and fracture parameter evaluation of notched specimens made from basalt fiber /glass fiber hybrid composite laminates
detail.abstract: In practical engineering applications, surface scratch defects are inevitably introduced into basalt fiber/glass fiber hybrid composite laminates. Under sustained external loading, these defects may progressively evolve into fracture failure, posing a potential threat to structural safety. To address this issue, a closed-form nonlinear fracture mechanics solution is employed to predict the fracture performance of hybrid composite laminates containing initial scratch defects. Based on the load-displacement curves of three-point bending specimens and CT image analysis of representative specimens, the fracture process consists of a linear stage, a softening stage, and a failure stage. By comparing normal, Weibull, and lognormal distributions, the normal distribution is identified as the most suitable model for describing the variability of fracture parameters. Accordingly, fracture parameters are statistically evaluated at a 95% confidence level. By comparing different parameter evaluation strategies, the characteristic composite unit [[EQUATION]] defined using the weighted average method exhibits higher prediction accuracy within the scope of the present study. The tensile strength [[EQUATION]] and equivalent crack [[EQUATION]] first increase and then decrease with increasing crack-thickness ratio [[EQUATION]] within the tested range. Furthermore, under the investigated material system and loading condition, the fracture behavior of full-size specimens can be reasonably predicted using parameters derived from a single set of small-scale notched specimens, indicating the potential applicability of the proposed approach for predicting the fracture performance of large composite structural components.

title: Migration and Long-Term Demographic Change: Can We Control the Numbers?
affiliations: Monash University and Paderborn University

detail.title: Migration and Long-Term Demographic Change: Can We Control the Numbers?
detail.abstract: In many Western societies, mass immigration has been one of the most divisive policy issues in recent years. Seemingly moderate inflows of migrants can have substantial demographic consequences in the long run, due to (1) higher fertility of the migrant population, (2) its younger age distribution, and (3) the possibility of family reunification. Yet, demography hardly appears in the policy debate, even in media outlets that are critical of mass immigration. This may indicate that the mechanics of population dynamics are not widely understood. We design a laboratory experiment in which we confront subjects with 30 different migration scenarios. Subjects have to decide when to stop a given inflow of migrants to achieve a target share of migrants after 60 years. In line with all our pre-registered hypotheses, in scenarios that contain elements of usual mass immigration the growth of the migrant population is systematically underestimated. This bias is even stronger in scenarios that closely resemble the German situation since the opening of the borders during the 2015 refugee crisis.

title: Transitional Justice and Human Rights: The Role of Lawyers in Promoting Accountability and Reconciliation

detail.title: Transitional Justice and Human Rights: The Role of Lawyers in Promoting Accountability and Reconciliation
detail.abstract:
Transitional justice is a mechanism in human rights protection developed to help societies rectify large-scale human rights violations, ensuring accountability, serving justice and bringing reconciliation to the victims of the human rights violations and the society at large (Secretary-General, United Nations, 2010). The process involves a range of permanent and temporary institutions and state or non-state actors. These participants may be international and domestic institutions, such as courts, ad hoc tribunals, commissions of inquiry, non-governmental organizations, and even key stakeholders such as lawyers (Jeffery and Dannhauer, 2024), (Chenou et al., 2019).

Importantly, lawyers play an important role in achieving the promotion of accountability and reconciliation in instances of human rights violations post-conflict situations. This is because lawyers are a necessity in the justice system. In this article, the critical roles that lawyers play is examined vis-à-vis the intersection of transitional justice and human rights.

title: Sociogrowth and Whiteness as Growth
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Sociogrowth and Whiteness as Growth
detail.abstract: Growthism is cardinal and core to contemporary society, particularly under capitalist regimes where wealth accumulation and resource exploitation are pursued with a logic of infinite expansion. Degrowth scholars have engaged in both academic and activist deliberations on the dangers of perpetual economic growth, forming political coalitions and producing a range of literature. What critiques of growth often lack is a sociological and critical race theory lens, or references to race altogether, despite the very nature of capitalism being racialized. In this paper, whiteness is understood as having developed alongside growthist capitalism, not as isolated instruments but as an aggregate. In fact, whiteness has and continues to operate ideologically and materially as growth. From chattel slavery and land theft to the wages of whiteness, this racial invention is deeply tied to economic growth, and transcending white dominance and growth economics must be pursued in tandem.

title: The Stock Market Participation Puzzle: What Do We Know and Where Do We Go from Here?
affiliations: Monash University, Universiti Utara Malaysia and Universiti Utara Malaysia

detail.title: The Stock Market Participation Puzzle: What Do We Know and Where Do We Go from Here?

publicationDetails.detailsText: No, the paper has not been accepted anywhere

detail.abstract: We review the literature on the stock market participation puzzle, which is the phenomenon that many households do not invest in stocks. Participation is around 37 percent in the US and is much lower in most other countries, especially in developing economics. Explanations include a lack of financial literacy, sociability, trust, health, and cognitive abilities. Given that most of these factors are correlated, we suggest that future studies focus on finding a hierarchy of explanations that explain the puzzle.

title: Maintaining Reality Contact in Bounded Systems: Suppression, Distortion, and Proxy Hijack
affiliations: UNSW Business School

detail.title: Maintaining Reality Contact in Bounded Systems: Suppression, Distortion, and Proxy Hijack
detail.abstract: Finite agents act through representations that incompletely track the generative processes they depend on. Some mismatch is therefore inevitable. The practical problem is not error per se, but degradation of the discrepancy channels that normally maintain reality contact. I propose a compact topology of discrepancy-driven failure in bounded systems, distinguishing three loci: suppression (relevant discrepancies fail to enter updating), distortion (discrepancies are systematically recoded before revision), and proxy hijack (optimisation concentrates on a proxy signal that is imperfectly coupled to the latent objective). The framework organises dispersed phenomena across psychology, organisations, economics, and artificial systems around discrepancy-channel integrity rather than domain-specific mechanisms. It generates dissociable process signatures, regime conditions for proxy-latent divergence, and mode-matched intervention predictions. The analysis motivates truth literacy as a transferable competence for preserving corrigibility under uncertainty.

title: Decentralized Admissibility: Slack, Inheritance, and the Necessity of Memory
affiliations: Friedrich Schiller University - Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science

detail.title: Decentralized Admissibility: Slack, Inheritance, and the Necessity of Memory
detail.abstract:
This paper studies the persistence of admissibility in decentralized environments with population turnover and verification lag. At each date, spatial robustness requires that an alternative be supported by at least k agents providing η-interior slack. We show that when admissibility depends only on contemporaneous signals-historyblindness-verification lag generates a structural handoff gap. Even if primitive slack is perfectly preserved across time, the replacement of a verified agent by an entrant can render a previously pivotal alternative inadmissible. The failure is purely informational: contemporaneous signals are not a sufficient statistic for preserved primitive slack. 
We prove that no history-blind, spatially robust rule can guarantee continuity across such handoffs. Restoring persistence requires enlarging the informational domain. We characterize the Public Core-the set of previously admissible alternatives-as the minimal public state that bridges verification lag. Institutional memory is therefore not an auxiliary feature of decentralized design, but an informational lower bound imposed by verification frictions.

detail.abstract: This paper develops corporate-state metabolism to explain how public institutions absorb and transform governance technologies first tested in private-order settings. It traces a long arc from feudal and mercantile instruments (contracts, accounting, merchant courts) into early public law, and reads the American founding as a metabolic condenser that repackaged colonial self-government, corporate charters, and religious associational templates into scalable constitutional architecture. In the digital era, a pressure gradient between fast enterprise systems and slow public workflows drives states toward ERP, portals, and case-management platforms-while importing risks of vendor lock-in, surveillance, and bureaucratic self-preservation. The paper argues that bureaucracies selectively adopt tools that protect resources and discretion while resisting those that increase responsibility or make failure legible; when external filters weaken, the system can cross a threshold into a terminal bureaucracy that drains a weakening society and collapses into fragmented, oligarchic order.

detail.abstract: The rapid urbanization and increasing complexity of modern cities demand innovative approaches to emergency response. This study investigates how Next-Generation 911 (NG911) systems can be optimized through the integration of real-time geospatial analytics and predictive routing algorithms. By synthesizing empirical research, system simulations, and GIS-based data analyses, the study evaluates how real-time mapping, sensor integration, and AI-driven routing enhance response times and resource allocation. Findings indicate that NG911 systems equipped with detailed geospatial analytics reduce average response times by 15-25%, improve emergency resource distribution, and increase operational resilience. Unexpected limitations, such as incomplete indoor maps and signal interference in urban environments, were identified as key areas requiring further research. The study concludes that effective NG911 optimization requires a holistic integration of geospatial intelligence, predictive analytics, and continuous data updates. Policymakers and emergency management agencies must prioritize investment in AI-enhanced GIS systems and inter-agency data sharing to maximize public safety outcomes

title: Heatwaves, Coldwaves, Floods, and Droughts: The Short-Term Impact of Extreme Weather Events on Economic Activity
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Heatwaves, Coldwaves, Floods, and Droughts: The Short-Term Impact of Extreme Weather Events on Economic Activity
detail.abstract: This paper examines the short-term macroeconomic and sectoral effects of extreme weather events in Germany, France, Italy, and Spain. We construct novel indicators of extreme temperature and precipitation based on percentile thresholds of long-run historical distributions and estimate their impact through country-specific structural Bayesian VAR models. The analysis documents sizable and heterogeneous effects on real GDP, HICP, and sectoral activity over a one-year horizon. Temperature extremes primarily affect industrial and energy-related sectors, with Germany exhibiting the strongest vulnerability to heatwaves. Precipitation extremes mainly impact construction and mining, with Spain featuring the largest exposure to floods and droughts. Sectoral composition plays a key role in shaping transmission, with pharmaceuticals, electricity, construction, and mining displaying distinct and recurrent patterns. Given their impact on prices, extreme weather event shocks may exert inflationary pressures without hurting activity, or induce demand-type of effects on the overall economy, with different effects across countries.

title: Housing Wealth and Monetary Policy Transmission: Cross-Country Evidence
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Housing Wealth and Monetary Policy Transmission: Cross-Country Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the role of housing wealth in the transmission of monetary policy to consumption in 20 advanced economies. Using Bayesian VAR models we identify structural shocks with a novel combination of sign and maximum forecast error variance restrictions, isolating the housing wealth channel through counterfactual impulse responses. We find that the housing wealth multiplier — the sensitivity of consumption to exogenous house price changes — is strongly correlated with outright homeownership rates and is higher for durable consumption. Cross-country differences in the monetary policy transmission to consumption are largely driven by the cash-flow channel.

title: Managerial Investment and Innovation Transmission in Chinese Manufacturing: Multi-Level Evidence from Firms and Innovation Sectors
affiliations: and University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences

detail.title: Managerial Investment and Innovation Transmission in Chinese Manufacturing: Multi-Level Evidence from Firms and Innovation Sectors
detail.abstract: Amid narrowing profit margins and intensifying competition in Chinese manufacturing, understanding how innovation is transmitted across firms and production units is essential for explaining industrial upgrading. This paper introduces the concept of innovation sectors beyond traditional industry classifications and constructs a multi-level dataset linking firms to innovation sectors. Using longitudinal firm data from 2003–2014 combined with innovation output indicators in 2025, we employ a two-stage trend estimation approach to examine how long-term input structures affect innovation transmission. The results show that persistent managerial investment significantly promotes innovation transmission at both firm and innovation-sector levels, whereas asset accumulation does not exhibit a stable positive effect. These findings suggest that innovation diffusion in Chinese manufacturing follows a hierarchical and nested pattern: innovation capabilities spread not through capital expansion alone but through organizational accumulation and resource reallocation across firms and sectors. The study provides new multi-level evidence on China’s transition from scale-driven to innovation-driven manufacturing and offers implications for policies aimed at fostering sustainable industrial upgrading.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes "Topological Global Economics," a dimensional expansion of "Governance Engineering"—previously established for regional resource cycles—to a planetary scale. We formulate the "Flat-Earth Fallacy" inherent in contemporary macroeconomics, which assumes an infinite space where entropy can be discarded externally, ignoring the physical constraints of the Earth's finite surface area (4²). On a closed Riemannian manifold, the dynamic N-Body Problem of economic agents exhibits deterministic chaos; however, we provide a rigorous structural solution by redefining it as a problem of geometric stability via Additively Weighted Spherical Tessellation. Through the construction of a "Planetary Replica" using the economic mass of G7 nations and China, we identify "Economic Fault Lines" arising from the misalignment of mass distribution. Crucially, our model provides a causal geometric explanation for the "residuals" observed in empirical trade networks that traditional gravity models fail to account for. We formalize international trade as a "pressure adjustment valve" at polygon interfaces and conflict as a physical "Structural Buckling" of the system. Furthermore, by defining oceans as "Superconducting Areas" with zero physical resistance, we prove the existence of autonomous multipolar equilibria governed by an invariant autonomy coefficient (a ≈ 0.12). This research moves beyond political rhetoric to offer engineering specifications for a "Planetary OS"—a sustainable, high-velocity resource circulation circuit governed by physical boundary conditions.

title: Signaling Without Signals: Arena Choice Under AI Homogenization
affiliations: Kwansei Gakuin University - School of Sociology

detail.title: Signaling Without Signals: Arena Choice Under AI Homogenization
