declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 25K05449.

detail.abstract: When AI homogenizes output, traditional performance signals lose their informational value, and evaluators revert to prior beliefs about social origin, reproducing the condition for statistical discrimination through a different mechanism. We show that individuals respond by strategically choosing costly evaluation arenas that AI cannot homogenize, producing a Spence-type signaling game. We derive the Riley separating equilibrium in closed form under a broad class of cost functions and show that equilibrium payoffs are independent of both the cost parameter and the cost functional form. When prior beliefs are sufficiently favorable, all types prefer the pooling outcome, yet the D1 refinement selects the separating equilibrium, producing a prisoner's dilemma in which signaling makes everyone worse off. Because payoffs are cost-invariant, subsidizing or restricting arena access is ineffective; the model points instead to raising the floor of the ability distribution as the relevant policy lever.

title: Anomaly-Driven Demand
affiliations: Aarhus University - CREATES and Aarhus University - Department of Economics and Business Economics

detail.title: Anomaly-Driven Demand
detail.abstract: We show that trading on anomalies generates price pressure in the underlying stocks. We construct a proxy for anomaly-driven demand (ADD), capturing demand generated when investors rebalance into and out of anomaly long and short legs. Stocks with high ADD earn significantly higher subsequent returns than stocks with low ADD. This effect carries over to anomalies: anomalies whose constituent stocks have the highest ADD earn 8.04 percentage points higher annualized returns than those whose contituent stocks have the lowest ADD. These results suggest that investor demand for anomalies induce price pressure that becomes incorporated into observed anomaly returns.

title: Regional Features of Demographic Dynamics in the Republic of Karelia: Current State and Trends

detail.title: Regional Features of Demographic Dynamics in the Republic of Karelia: Current State and Trends
detail.abstract:
The Republic of Karelia faces a profound demographic crisis characteristic of many subjects within the Northwestern Federal District, yet possessing distinct regional specifics. This study analyzes the dynamics of population size, components of reproduction, and the effectiveness of regional demographic policy for the period 2000–2024.

Statistical analysis reveals a monotonic population decline from 735.5 thousand persons in 2000 to 523.9 thousand in 2024, representing a decrease of 28.8%. Key findings indicate a sustained fertility decline following a 2014 peak, with the Total Fertility Rate reaching 1.35 in 2023, significantly below the replacement level. Mortality rates remain consistently above the national average (16.4‰ in 2023), driven primarily by circulatory diseases and external causes. Consequently, natural population decline reached –8.1‰ in 2024, one of the highest rates in the Russian Federation. Although a migration inflow was recorded from 2021 to 2024 (+3.5–4.1‰), it fails to compensate for natural loss.

The study examines the decentralized governance structure of demographic policy and existing support measures, including maternity capital and family benefits. While social support systems are preserved and migration outflow trends reversed post-2021, critical challenges persist: high mortality among working-age men, absence of long-term migrant retention strategies, and a shrinking cohort of women of fertile age.

The paper concludes that financial incentives alone are insufficient to ensure demographic sustainability. Recommendations include implementing regional programs to reduce suicidality and alcohol consumption, developing psychological support services, creating comprehensive migrant adaptation packages, and enhancing housing policies for young families. Sustainable demographic development in Karelia depends on the integrated improvement of infrastructure, labor markets, and public health preservation measures.

title: Ambition as Insurance: When Task Choice Protects Self-Belief

detail.abstract: Individuals sometimes choose highly ambitious tracks despite low success probabilities. This note proposes an informational mechanism: when failure in extremely competitive environments is less diagnostic of ability than failure in moderately competitive ones, ambitious choice functions as insurance against adverse belief updating. A closed-form characterization of the belief-insurance threshold shows that ambitious choice becomes more attractive when the diagnosticity gap between tasks is large, when the prior probability of high ability is high, and when material stakes are low. Risk-taking in this framework arises not from convex utility but from differences in informational structure.

detail.abstract: The 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns created a global "natural experiment" in atmospheric science, temporarily decoupling economic activity from environmental degradation. This study evaluates PM2.5 and NO₂ concentrations across five global megacities-New York, London, Delhi, Beijing, and Tokyo-between 2018 and 2022. By analyzing the "accidental" air quality gains of 2020 against the subsequent "rebound" in 2021-2022, the research demonstrates that long-term recovery is not a byproduct of technology alone but a direct indicator of institutional governance capacity. The study concludes that cities with robust regulatory enforcement maintained structural declines, while cities with reactive policies experienced a total return to pre-pandemic pollution levels.

title: Functional Newton Solution for Heterogeneous-Agent DSGE Models Wealth Distribution and Consumption Dynamics in OECD Economies (2000-2025)
affiliations: University of Ain Temouchent

detail.title: Functional Newton Solution for Heterogeneous-Agent DSGE Models Wealth Distribution and Consumption Dynamics in OECD Economies (2000-2025)
detail.abstract: This study develops a nonlinear heterogeneous agent macroeconomic framework to analyze wealth distribution dynamics, consumption transmission mechanisms, and policy stabilization performance. The model integrates advanced numerical solution techniques based on Functional Newton equilibrium solvers to make large scale heterogeneous agent dynamic stochastic general equilibrium simulation computationally feasible. Simulation results for United States and selected advanced economies show that wealth heterogeneity plays a central role in determining macroeconomic volatility, fiscal multiplier effectiveness, and monetary policy transmission asymmetry. Tail households with high marginal propensity to consume generate nonlinear amplification effects in aggregate demand fluctuations, especially under liquidity constraint regimes. Policy experiment analysis demonstrates that distribution targeted fiscal interventions outperform uniform transfer policies in terms of welfare improvement, inequality reduction, and stabilization efficiency. Robustness tests confirm structural stability of the nonlinear dynamic system under variations in risk aversion, borrowing limits, and shock persistence parameters. Computational performance evaluation shows that the Functional Newton solution method provides fast convergence, high precision policy mapping, and scalable heterogeneous agent macroeconomic simulation capability. The framework enables realistic large scale welfare and distributional policy assessment. Overall, the research provides theoretical, numerical, and policy contributions to nonlinear macroeconomic modeling with heterogeneous agents.

title: Incentive Design with Biased Reviewers and Compensation Committee
affiliations: Meiji University and Keio University - Graduate School of Business Administration

detail.title: Incentive Design with Biased Reviewers and Compensation Committee
detail.abstract: This paper studies incentive design in organizations that rely on subjective performance evaluation and bonus pools when evaluation is delegated to a potentially biased reviewer and overseen by a compensation committee. We develop a repeated-game model in which a principal commits to a single-step, fixed-sum reward scheme that splits a bonus pool between winners and losers. A reviewer observes a noisy, rank-based performance signal and proposes a permutation of prizes, which is implemented only if approved by a committee that follows a costly approval rule. Reviewer and agents interact repeatedly, so relational contracts discipline favoritism and shirking through continuation values. The single-step architecture yields a simple static backbone that maps the prize spread into equilibrium effort. Holding governance levers fixed, we first characterize an interior benchmark in which committee and governance costs alone determine the optimal prize spread and effort. We then derive a reviewer-constrained frontier that caps the maximum sustainable spread when the reviewer is tempted to favor preferred agents. The globally implementable spread is the minimum of these two and generates a regime classification. Comparative statics show how approval strictness, reviewer rotation, and evaluation coarseness jointly shape effort provision and the value of committee oversight.

title: Execution Latency in Inventory Control: Extending Reorder Point Logic to Organizational Reality

detail.title: Execution Latency in Inventory Control: Extending Reorder Point Logic to Organizational Reality

detail.abstract: Classical or Traditional inventory models such as Economic Reorder Quantity (EOQ) and Reorder Point (ROP) structures conjecture that replenishment actions are executed immediately once predefined thresholds or maybe a start point is reached. While this model is frequently used in all places but when seeing through mathematical sense or using a analytical thinking, this assumption frequently fails in practice, particularly in emergingmarket procurement environments where variables like hierarchical approvals, budget constraints, and procedural compliance play an important role in characterization of the process. As an outcome, the organization faces stockouts, emergency sourcing, and cost escalation even when the text book policies are accurately applied. This paper reasons that these failures origin from a systematic misunderstanding of lead time in classical inventory theory. This classical inventory models treat lead time only as an external variable factor, which is driven by the supplier. While abandoning predictable and deterministic variables such as internal decision delays immersed in organizational procurement process. Depicting on classical inventory theory, bounded rationality, and emerging-market supply chain literature, this study reimagines lead time as the sum of external supplier lead time and internal decision lead time. An execution-aware inventory structure is presented that differentiates between inventory signals that trigger organizational process and those that trigger order placement. New constructs or variables including the Execution Recognition Threshold (ERT), Authority-Constrained Order Quantity (ACOQ), and Emergency Risk Zone (ERZ)-are presented to capture the execution-level limitations or constraints faced by procurement professionals. And a numerical illustration that reveals that the classical inventory theory faced reorder points often initiate action only after the organization has entered a high-risk zone, while execution-aware triggers absorb internal delays without increasing safety stock. This study does not reject classical or traditional inventory theory and its models; rather, it extends them by aligning reorder logic with execution actuality. These finding call attention to the need to shift inventory control from buffer-based firefighting toward process-aware design, with suggestions for inventory theory, procurement practice, and supply chain education, particularly in emerging-market contexts.

title: Algorithms, Biases, and Biryani: Behavioral Economics of Tinder in Urban Bangladesh
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Algorithms, Biases, and Biryani: Behavioral Economics of Tinder in Urban Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
This paper examines digital matchmaking in urban Bangladesh through the lens of behavioral economics, using Tinder as a case study of algorithm-mediated decision-making under social and cultural constraints. While online dating platforms are often modeled as efficient matching markets, user behavior in Bangladesh deviates systematically from classical rational-choice predictions due to stigma, reputational concerns, and family oversight. Drawing on a mixed-methods approach that combines survey evidence, platform usage patterns, and qualitative interviews with urban users, this study analyzes how cognitive biases and social heuristics shape participation and choice.

The findings highlight the presence of present bias, choice overload, anchoring effects, and gendered selection heuristics, all of which interact with Tinder’s algorithmic ranking system to produce suboptimal and asymmetric matching outcomes. Market frictions such as ghosting, selective engagement, and urban–rural pool imbalances further constrain matching efficiency. These dynamics suggest that algorithmic nudges may amplify existing behavioral biases rather than correct them, particularly in socially restrictive environments.

By situating digital dating within a culturally constrained decision-making framework, this paper extends behavioral economics and matching theory to a non-Western context. The study contributes empirical insights into how technology, social norms, and human biases jointly shape outcomes in emerging digital markets, with implications for platform design, user welfare, and policy considerations related to algorithmic mediation in social interactions

We introduce the spacetime metric, based on General Relativity, as a direct economic metric, defining a cost function that integrates gravitational potential and proper time differentials.

title: Blowin' in the Wind? Adapting to Atlantic Basin Tropical Cyclones with Pesticides ⋆
affiliations: Deakin University

detail.title: Blowin' in the Wind? Adapting to Atlantic Basin Tropical Cyclones with Pesticides ⋆
detail.abstract:
Using U.S. county-level data, we uncover a relatively overlooked coping strategy employed by farmers in response to cyclones: selective increase of pesticide application. By constructing a novel dataset spanning 25 years of tropical cyclone activity, pesticide use, and agricultural output, our difference-in-differences design reveals that farmers respond to cyclone shocks by applying more pesticides to protect their crops. On average, a typical U.S. farm applies approximately 2,150–2,250 kg more pesticides in both the event year and the following - around ten times the normal annual quantity. While rising pesticide use poses health and environmental risks, our heterogeneity analysis offers a more nuanced view. Farmers
selectively boost pesticide applications to counter the rise in pests and pathogens that usually follow cyclones. They raise the use of lower-toxicity pesticides (e.g., 2,4-D, Metolachlor) but not highly hazardous ones (e.g., Chlorpyrifos), suggesting endogenous avoidance behavior consistent with risk awareness and regulatory constraints. These results hold robustly across eight measures of cyclone intensity, including rainfall, wind speed, and duration. In terms of coping mechanisms, farmers not only intensify pesticide use on existing crops but also expand their harvested acreage to compensate for yield losses, with effects lasting up to four years after a cyclone event. Overall, our results indicate that pesticide intensification, though adaptive in the short term, imposes considerable e and environmental trade-offs.

title: Asset Prices, Bubbles and Monetary Policy
affiliations: The University of Tokyo

detail.title: Asset Prices, Bubbles and Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: In this paper, we provide a Dynamic New Keynesian (DNK) framework that incorporates rational asset bubbles into an economy featuring a financial accelerator mechanism driven by binding collateral constraints. Using this model, we revisit the debate on optimal monetary policy responses to asset prices and bubbles. In this economy, entrepreneurs possess heterogeneous efficiency in operating physical capital and face a collateral constraint that limits their borrowing capacity based on the value of their physical capital holdings. Intrinsically useless bubble assets are traded in the entrepreneur sector, which facilitate the transfer of resources from inefficient to efficient entrepreneurs, thereby sustaining a positive value. A central feature of the short-run economic dynamics is that both price of physical capital and bubbles interact with entrepreneurs' net worth, endogenously affecting the tightness of financial constraints. By minimizing the central bank's loss function, we find that the optimal policy response to the aggregate asset price index-comprising both value of physical capital and bubbles-is not uniform; it depends crucially on the source of exogenous shocks as well as the optimality of concurrent responses to inflation and the output gap, besides the relative weights assigned to the objectives under the central bank's dual mandate. Conversely, responding to asset bubbles in isolation is found to be suboptimal.

detail.abstract: This paper studies equilibrium determinacy in a growing New Keynesian economy in which fiscal policy targets the face value debt-to-GDP ratio and the government issues long-maturity nominal debt. Because the monitored debt stock is insensitive to market valuation while issuance costs depend on bond prices, expectations-driven movements in long-bond prices induce fiscal adjustment that feeds back to capital accumulation and inflation. The determinacy region is bounded above by an admissible policy constraint. Local determinacy requires the inflation response to lie above a maturity-based cutoff and below this admissible upper bound, which can be close to one. A two-instrument extension with an ultra short bond shows how rollover exposure and portfolio shares shift both bounds. Numerical exercises show that determinacy may require an inflation coefficient only slightly above one together with a sizable output-gap response, and that longer maturity can tighten the determinate set relative to the flexible price benchmark.

detail.abstract: In markets where intermediation requires deploying capital at risk under genuine uncertainty, the equilibrium price of intermediation has a strictly positive floor. Three channels contribute to this floor: (i) the participation constraint on risk-bearing capital, which requires compensation for irreducible risk (Sharpe, 1964); (ii) market clearing under finite capital supply, which prices the opportunity cost of balance sheet commitment; and (iii) the Grossman-Stiglitz (1980) information cost paradox, which prevents full revelation of costly-to-acquire information. AI-driven automation compresses transaction and information-processing costs but does not eliminate the underlying capital requirement, the scarcity of balance sheet, or the cost of producing genuinely new information. The binding constraint rotates across regimes—the participation constraint dominates in high-volatility environments, capital scarcity binds during balance-sheet contractions, and the information floor binds in opaque or novel markets—implying that the composite floor persists even when any individual channel is slack.

This study examines integrated strategies for food security defense management and the organized rescue of at-risk populations in scenarios of nuclear war and mass atrocities. By synthesizing insights from disaster management, humanitarian logistics, and international law, the research proposes a multilayered framework that includes resilient food supply chains, strategic stockpiling, rapid distribution systems, and community-based defense mechanisms. detail.abstract: This paper studies the causal impact of female political representation on legislative behavior, social attitudes, and gender-based crime. Using a regression discontinuity design based on close mixed-gender electoral contests, we compare electorates that narrowly elected female versus male candidates. We link computational text analysis of parliamentary debates, roll-call votes, post-election survey responses, and administrative police records from 2010 to 2022 in Australia. We document three main findings. First, female MPs devote significantly more attention to gender-related issues in parliamentary speech and are more likely to support gender-related legislation, including measures addressing gender-based violence, with no evidence of differential voting absence. Second, exposure to a narrowly elected female MP shifts constituent attitudes toward greater support for women's rights. Third, electorates that narrowly elect a female MP experience a statistically and economically meaningful decline in gendered crime rates during the subsequent term. Together, the results indicate that female representation can shape policy priorities, social attitudes, and downstream gendered outcomes, even within a disciplined party system.

detail.abstract:
Music metadata increasingly shapes remuneration accuracy and cultural visibility in AI- and platform-mediated markets, yet the European metadata landscape remains structurally fragmented due to territorial rights management, divergent identifier systems, and proprietary data silos. This article argues that the resulting failures – namely unmatched royalties, inefficient licensing, and distorted discoverability – are best understood as a governance problem rather than a purely technical deficit. It therefore reframes the “music metadata dilemma” as a question of institutional design and evaluates whether a decentralised data space architecture, consistent with the logic of the EU’s Common European Data Spaces (CEDS) initiative, may offer a more viable alternative to repository-centred solutions in a rights-sensitive and commercially contested sector.

Examining this question through the lens of EU data and digital legislation, particularly the Open Data Directive (ODD), the Data Governance Act (DGA), and the Data Act (DA), and using the European Health Data Space (EHDS) as a methodological reference point, the article identifies the legal mechanisms most relevant to a prospective European music metadata space. These include interoperability obligations, constraints on unfair contractual terms, and intermediary governance structures. It also highlights persistent tensions created by the “without prejudice” architecture of EU data law vis-à-vis copyright and trade secrets. The article concludes by assessing the extent to which the current EU data law framework can support governed interoperability for music metadata and where more targeted, sector-specific intervention may be required.

detail.abstract: Social e-commerce has emerged as a core application scenario in the digital economy, where consumer purchasing decisions heavily rely on multidimensional signals released by platforms and influencers. However, the mechanisms underlying trust formation remain under-explored. Existing research predominantly focuses on the linear effects of individual signals, overlooking the “endowment-incentive” heterogeneity in signal functions. It also neglects the configurational effects and asymmetric logic of trust formation, while methodologically being constrained by traditional linear analysis, failing to reveal complex causal relationships. This study integrates signal theory with the Two-Factor Theory, centering on five core signal elements including quasi-social interaction and information quality. Employing a mixed methodology of PLS-SEM, NCA, and fsQCA, it conducts empirical analysis based on 495 valid social e-commerce user samples. Findings reveal: CT serves as the core driver of PI, while AT functions defensively; SP is a prerequisite for high PI, high PI can be achieved through three configurational pathways—experiential interaction, social atmosphere reinforcement, and immersion compensation—while non-high PI is driven by the absence of core elements like SP and AT, FE selectively enhance the relationship between RC and CT. This study expands the application boundaries of signaling theory and dual-factor theory in the social e-commerce domain, refines the asymmetric configuration framework for trust formation, and provides precise practical guidance for platforms and content creators to optimize information strategies and enhance user purchase intent.

detail.abstract: Despite significant advancements in Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) technologies and the widespread adoption of standardized implementation methodologies, ERP projects continue to exhibit high rates of failure and underperformance. Existing research frequently attributes these outcomes to execution-level issues such as project management deficiencies, resistance to change, or inadequate training. However, such explanations often overlook deeper structural and institutional conditions that shape implementation outcomes. This study adopts a conceptual and applied research approach to examine ERP implementation failure through the lens of organizational governance and readiness. Drawing on recent academic literature and industry evidence, the paper introduces the concept of the procedural and governance disconnect to explain why ERP initiatives systematically fail despite technical maturity. The proposed framework conceptualizes ERP failure as the result of misalignment between implementation procedures, governance structures, and organizational readiness mechanisms. By reframing ERP implementation as a governance-enabled organizational capability rather than an IT-centric project, this research contributes a structural perspective to the ERP failure discourse. The findings offer practical implications for executives and governance bodies seeking to redesign ERP initiatives as enterprise-wide transformation programs. detail.abstract: To foster innovation, organisations increasingly rely on collaboration and knowledge exchange, both within and beyond their organisational boundaries. Collaborative innovation platforms (CIPs) have emerged as a key enabler of these innovation efforts. However, there is no overview of existing CIPs, leading to a fragmented understanding of their design and innovation mechanisms. To address this gap, we conducted a multivocal literature review, combining a systematic literature review with a content analysis of commercial CIPs. 78 papers have been included in the review, describing 70 unique CIPs. By identifying the core mechanisms characterising CIPs and synthesizing them into a consolidated conceptual framework, the study advances theories of innovation, knowledge management, and platform design, and introduces a taxonomy that supports practitioners in systematically understanding and operationalizing these mechanisms. A future research agenda has been proposed to advance CIPs, focusing on the use of state-of-the-art technologies and emerging innovation mechanisms.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Complements Open-Source Knowledge in Startup Growth
detail.abstract: Startups increasingly invest in artificial intelligence (AI) to accelerate innovation and scale, yet many fail to capture the promised returns-an "AI paradox" driven by high data, talent, and maintenance costs. We argue that startups can mitigate this paradox through open-source knowledge acquisition (OSKA), a capability to systematically access, assimilate, and recombine external technical knowledge from opensource ecosystems. Drawing on complementarity theory, we propose that AI capability and OSKA form a mutually reinforcing system: AI enhances startups' ability to discover and absorb open-source knowledge, while OSKA stabilizes and raises the productivity of AI investments by enabling continuous learning and rapid technological updating. We test these arguments using a novel firm-year panel of 65,549 North American startups (2015-2023) that links PitchBook financing histories, Revelio Labs resume-based human capital measures, and GitHub public event records capturing OSKA activities (forks, watches, issues, and issue comments). Results show that AI capability and OSKA exhibit robust performance complementarity: their interaction significantly improves startups' performance, measured by venture funding amount. Mechanism analyses indicate two channels: AI capability improves the conversion of OSKA into innovation outputs (e.g., software releases and trademarks), while OSKA reduces AI-talent attrition and increases innovation output per unit of AI labor investment. Together, the findings explain heterogeneous returns to AI and highlight the strategic importance of co-investing in internal AI talent and external open-source learning.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between algorithmic content curation on social media platforms and voter behavior across four election cycles in Georgia (2018, 2020, 2022, 2024). Using a county-year panel dataset combining official election outcomes with sentiment and topic analyses of over 2,000 political advertisements from Facebook's Ad Library, we examine how algorithmically delivered content correlates with voter turnout and partisan vote margins. Employing TextBlob for sentiment analysis and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for topic modeling, we quantify the emotional valence and thematic frames of political advertisements weighted by impression counts. Panel regression models with county and year fixed effects reveal that exposure to more negative, partisan-framed advertising content is associated with increased partisan vote margins (a 1.4 percentage point increase per standard deviation decrease in sentiment), though effects on turnout were modest and statistically insignificant. The influence of emotionally charged advertisements appears strongest during presidential election years. These findings provide ecological-level evidence that personalized, algorithm-driven political content may contribute to reinforcing partisan divides, with implications for platform governance and democratic discourse. detail.abstract: AI systems increasingly construct probabilistic models of human preference what we term behavioral digital twins by continuously updating estimates of internal states from observable behavioral signals. We argue that Kalman filtering, the mathematical framework underlying optimal state estimation in engineering systems, provides a theoretically precise and practically illuminating lens for analyzing how these systems work, how they fail, and why their failures follow predictable patterns that existing critical algorithm scholarship has not fully characterized. Drawing on control systems engineering principles, we identify five failure modes endemic to deployed behavioral estimation systems: model drift, filter divergence and filter bubble formation, time constant compression, self-reinforcing feedback instability, and measurement corruption through adversarial and economic disturbance. We argue these failures are not incidental but structurally determined by misaligned objective functions systems optimized for platform engagement rather than accurate preference estimation will produce systematically biased estimates as a mathematical necessity. We give particular attention to Generation Synthetica children born circa 2021 onward who will mature entirely within persistently adaptive estimation environments. For this cohort, behavioral digital twins are not optional features but developmental infrastructure, raising under examined questions about cognitive externalization, identity formation, and democratic competence. We conclude by proposing a governance framework derived from safety-critical engineering practice, arguing that systems affecting children's cognitive development warrant oversight proportional to that responsibility.

Design/methodology/approach: This study, through a mixed-method research design, analysed data collected from 81 schools, sampled from 501 educational institutions, operating with Academic Bridge, a Rwandan-based school data management SaaS platform, from 2020 to 2024. A structured questionnaire was used to collect quantitative data, which was studied through regression analysis, and semi-structured interviews were used to collect qualitative data from platform staff.

Practical implications: In emerging markets, the SaaS providers need to focus on investment in localised and multilingual support systems, through multi-modal accessibility, that go beyond solving technical issues to active outreach, in-country training, and culturally relevant communication tools like WhatsApp and phone support.

Originality/value: The research presents empirical evidence of the effectiveness of user support in an African SaaS setting, which illustrates that relationship-based models of support are key competitive differentiators when users have high levels of barriers to digital adoption.

detail.abstract: Frontier LLM companies have repeatedly assured courts and regulators that their models do not store copies of training data. They further rely on safety alignment strategies via RLHF, system prompts, and output filters to block verbatim regurgitation of copyrighted works, and have cited the efficacy of these measures in their legal defenses against copyright infringement claims. We show that finetuning bypasses these protections: by training models to expand plot summaries into full text, a task naturally suited for commercial writing assistants, we cause GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 to reproduce up to 85-90% of held-out copyrighted books, with single verbatim spans exceeding 460 words, using only semantic descriptions as prompts and no actual book text. This extraction generalizes across authors: finetuning exclusively on Haruki Murakami's novels unlocks verbatim recall of copyrighted books from over 30 unrelated authors. The effect is not specific to any training author or corpus: random author pairs and public-domain finetuning data produce comparable extraction, while finetuning on synthetic text yields near-zero extraction, indicating that finetuning on individual authors' works reactivates latent memorization from pretraining. Three models from different providers memorize the same books in the same regions (r ≥ 0.90), pointing to an industry-wide vulnerability. Our findings offer compelling evidence that model weights store copies of copyrighted works and that the security failures that manifest after finetuning on individual authors' works undermine a key premise of recent fair use rulings, where courts have conditioned favorable outcomes on the adequacy of measures preventing reproduction of protected expression.

detail.abstract:
Set in December 2017, this case follows Tyler Lawson, an engineering manager at Fortune 200 technology firm. Lawson thrived under the leadership of his previous manager, Jake Fierro, who shielded Lawson from office politics and gave him a high amount of autonomy. Introduction

It was 6:45 a.m. on a crisp December morning in 2017 when Tyler Lawson swiped his security badge at Mountebank Systems' (Mountebank's) sprawling headquarters. On his way to the elevator, he stopped several times to chat with colleagues. Optimistic and gregarious, Lawson was on friendly terms with people in many different departments. However, as the elevator ascended, unease settled in. Another monthly report for his skip-level manager, Vice President of Network Infrastructure Steve Schultz, awaited completion—the latest request in a string of others that felt less like supportive oversight and more like a complete waste of time.

For the past year, Lawson had spearheaded the company's ambitious migration from Amazon Web Services (AWS) to Microsoft Azure, a massive undertaking promising to fundamentally improve the speed and reliability of Mountebank's systems for a fraction of the cost of AWS. Under ideal circumstances, it would have been a demanding project. But for three months, Lawson felt he'd spent more time defending the project's legitimacy in endless meetings and spreadsheet justifications than actually driving its technical execution forward. The engineering challenges felt solvable; the executive resistance felt increasingly intractable.

A year prior, a project of this magnitude would have filled Lawson with adrenaline. Now, at 34, he felt the distinct friction of organizational politics. He had built a reputation as Mountebank's fix-it prodigy: the engineer who slashed notification-system latency by 40% in 2014 and architected the fault-tolerant data-storage system that earned Mountebank a prestigious CIO Award the following year. But those victories had a noteworthy, now absent, component: Jake Fierro, the manager who had not only championed Lawson's technical vision but masterfully navigated the corporate landscape on his behalf.

title: Numeraire Construction in Multi-Currency Historical Data: Evidence from Early Modern Art Auctions, 1690–1859

detail.title: Numeraire Construction in Multi-Currency Historical Data: Evidence from Early Modern Art Auctions, 1690–1859
detail.abstract: Economic historians routinely face a practical challenge: how to combine price records denominated in different currencies—for example, splicing pre-revolutionary French livres with post-Napoleonic British pounds when no overlapping observations exist. Using 351,846 art auction transactions from the Getty Provenance Index (1690–1859), we clarify when numeraire choice matters and when it does not. First, when currency fixed effects are included, native-unit and silver-equivalent specifications yield identical residuals: conversion reparameterizes intercepts but adds no information. Second, when currency controls are unavailable—because a currency is sparse or appears only out-of-sample—unit harmonization matters substantially. In leave-one-currency-out exercises, direct estimation in a common numeraire reduces prediction error by 14–34% (20% on average). Unit harmonization is therefore redundant when currency coverage is complete but essential for dataset splicing and sparse-currency settings—conditions frequently encountered when constructing long-run price and wage series.

detail.title: Minimum Wage and Employment Stickiness: Cross-Country Evidence
detail.abstract: We investigate whether increases in minimum wages reduce employment stickiness. Using a crosscountry panel dataset of statutory minimum wage changes, we find that increases in minimum wages are associated with a reduction in employment stickiness. Subsample analyses further show that our result is more pronounced among low-technology firms, financially distressed firms, and firms with low cash liquidity. Moreover, our result is stronger when minimum wage growth exceeds inflation and in countries with stricter employment protection legislation. These patterns are consistent with managers allocating labor resources more carefully in response to rising wage floors. In addition, we find that reductions in employment stickiness translate into higher labor investment efficiency, improved labor productivity, and a lower likelihood of future layoffs, consistent with our main findings. Overall, we contribute to the ongoing debate on the labor-market consequences of minimum wage increases by providing novel evidence that minimum wage policies may enhance managerial efficiency in workforce planning.

detail.title: Enforcement Speeds In DeFi: Limits to a Race Against Time
detail.abstract: Retrospective blacklist enforcement fails structurally in permissionless systems: adversaries create wallets offline at negligible cost while enforcement designates addresses on-chain at finite bandwidth, an asymmetry no improvement in investigation speed can resolve. We document this using the complete population of 173 OFAC-sanctioned Ethereum wallets. Across approximately $3.3 billion in total wallet value, we document two structural enforcement failures. First, approximately 71% of value, equivalent to approximately $2.4 billion, exits before designation. Second, around one-fifth of address-token pairs continue transacting after sanctioning, including autonomous smart contracts that cannot comply by design; for human-controlled wallets, the rate is around 8%. Only 1.47% of blacklisted balances remain frozen. A race-condition model shows these failures are architectural rather than operational: the investigation window gives adversaries a head start that no increase in investigation speed can eliminate, because wallet creation is free while enforcement is bandwidth-constrained. A second independent result shows that even zero investigation lag leaves enforcement incomplete due to computational complexity in transaction graph tracing.

detail.title: A Metastable Regime of Oscillation Under Sustained Stretch
detail.abstract: This paper specifies Organizational Flow as a metastable oscillatory regime of the differentiated organizational system under sustained stretch. Contemporary organizations operate under persistent convergence pressure generated by velocity, evaluative intensity, and time compression. Under such conditions, some systems exhibit accelerating interpretive contraction and structural fragility, while others sustain distributed variance across successive decision cycles without collapse. This paper formalizes the latter as a distinct regime. Organizational Flow is not a psychological state scaled upward, nor a generic assertion that organizations are complex. It is a regime architecture defined by the interaction between convergence pressure and regulatory counterforces, preserved interpretive interval and structural variance safeguards, contingent on intact organizational metabolization capacity (OMC). The regime is bounded by nonlinear threshold dynamics and characterized by asymmetric collapse pathways: inertial compression is self-reinforcing, whereas oscillation is metastable and energy-dependent. The paper derives six propositions, delineates boundary conditions, and supplies operational and empirical pathways for testing the regulatory function across longitudinal decision cycles.

detail.title: From Participation to Action: Why Collective Systems See More Than They Do-and What It Takes to Close the Gap
detail.abstract: Collective systems are routinely judged by participation levels. More voices are assumed to produce better outcomes. This paper shows that assumption is false. A comparative, document-grounded analysis of seven structurally distinct cases (participatory budgeting, community organizing, truth commissions, local agenda processes, air traffic control, self-managed nursing teams, and folk-school formation) reveals that participation and communication are present in every system examined, action-producing or not. What differentiates systems that reliably convert input into execution is the presence of three structural conditions: (1) bounded ownership of decisions and outcomes, (2) functional coordination aligned to a decision point, and (3) an explicit translation mechanism that converts input into execution. Systems lacking any one of these conditions stall at plans or testimony despite high participation. The analysis proceeds inductively from 55 coded excerpts clustered into pre-theoretical concept clusters before any framework was applied. The paper extends Weick's sensemaking framework by identifying the structural conditions under which interpreted meaning becomes executable action, generalizes Ostrom's institutional conditions beyond resource commons, and provides complexity leadership theory with the structural preconditions that emergent action requires. The model is refined as SEE-SENSE-OWN-ACT-RETURN, with OWN named as a discrete stage: the structural hinge between sensing and acting at which collective intelligence Morgan • From Participation to Action • SSRN Working Paper 2026 1 either becomes operational or remains documented. The complete configuration of bounded ownership, functional coordination, and translation mechanism is termed the execution architecture of a collective system. Practical implications for leadership, system design, and the architecture of community processes are developed.

title: Deliberate Innovation and the Visibility Gap: A Theory of Structural Accumulation Under Velocity-Calibrated Recognition

detail.title: Deliberate Innovation and the Visibility Gap: A Theory of Structural Accumulation Under Velocity-Calibrated Recognition
detail.abstract: Innovation scholarship privileges velocity. Its dominant frameworks, disruption, breakthrough, radical innovation, fast-follower strategy, favor patterns characterized by speed, signal intensity, and visible scaling. This velocity bias has not merely left a gap in theory. It has distorted how the field evaluates capability formation, producing blind spots around innovation that is slow, structural, and deliberately quiet. This paper identifies and formalizes a missing core category: deliberate innovation, defined as constraint-conditioned architectural accumulation that compounds beneath detection thresholds until performance discontinuities render it legible. Deliberate innovation is not incrementalism, exploitation, or stealth strategy. It is a distinct innovation archetype in which constraint drives architectural discipline, structural depth compounds through integration and variance compression, identity stability sustains formation through periods of weak recognition, and advantage becomes visible only when performance thresholds are crossed. The paper formalizes the visibility gap as the recognition distortion that underdetects this pattern in acceleration-prone environments, arising when evaluative systems calibrated to velocity privilege high-frequency indicators and discount low-signal structural formation. Five mechanisms specify how deliberate innovation produces weak observable signals during formation. Eight propositions and one hypothesis provide a testable framework spanning both formation and detection. By naming this pattern and specifying the evaluative conditions that obscure it, the paper argues that innovation theory's velocity bias has hidden from view a consequential class of competitive advantage formation.

detail.abstract: Background: Healthcare systems worldwide are facing rising service demands and increasing levels of burnout. This is alongside compounding pressures of significant workforce shortages, difficulties in retaining staff, and stunted career development opportunities. The concept of thriving at work shows considerable promise in responding to these issues. However, it has been under-researched in health services research at both a conceptual and organisational level. Therefore, a rapid review is warranted to help inform future research, policy and practical interventions that foster a thriving healthcare workforce. Aim: To identify how thriving at work is (i) conceptualised and operationalised in health services research and (ii) synthesise extant literature on thriving initiatives and their related outcomes in healthcare settings. Setting: International healthcare environments. Design: Rapid literature review. Methods: Following Cochrane rapid review methodology and PRISMA guidance, we will search five healthcare databases including MEDLINE; EMBASE; CINAHL Complete; HMIC; and PsycINFO for records published in English since 2012. One reviewer will independently screen all titles and abstracts and full-text retrievals for consistency in the selection process. A second reviewer will check 20% at both stages for consistency; disputes will be resolved by a third reviewer and team discussion. Data extraction will capture: study design, context and population, thriving definitions and interventions, outcomes achieved, and implementation considerations. Findings: Results will be thematically synthesised and mapped. Conclusion: This rapid review will identify how thriving at work is conceptualised and operationalised in health services research to support a sustainable, equitable and thriving healthcare workforce.

title: The Geometric Siphon: Emergent Capital Reallocation in Concentrated Liquidity Portfolios
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Geometric Siphon: Emergent Capital Reallocation in Concentrated Liquidity Portfolios
detail.abstract:
This paper identifies and formalises the Geometric Siphon, a previously undocumented mechanism in concentrated liquidity (CL) portfolio management. When multiple CL positions share depositor-level token balances and are autonomously rebalanced, the geometric mismatch between consecutive tick ranges produces token residuals that flow through the shared balance, creating capital transfers between independent positions without oracles, governance or additional gas cost.

I derive a closed-form expression for the geometric residual ΔR from the Uniswap V3 amount equations and prove that ΔR = 0 if and only if the tick range is unchanged. Any range change produces a non-zero residual that follows directly from the CL amount equations. The theorem is verified with a Foundry test suite running against unmodified Uniswap V3 contracts. Range changes produce measurable residuals (2,061 USDC in the test scenario), same-range rebalances produce zero (< 10⁻⁶ USD), and residuals scale linearly with position size (4× position → 4× residual, ratio 4.00).

Empirical analysis of 1,380 rebalance events across 39 positions, five depositor groups, two contract versions and seven days on Aerodrome (Base) reveals a two-mechanism structure: Stage 1 (geometric creation, ~5% of events) produces residuals via range changes that feed the shared dust pool; Stage 2 (dust pool redistribution, ~95% of events) redistributes accumulated dust through same-range rebalances governed by the position-to-pool liquidity ratio V/L. The overall decomposition D = ΔR − S holds at ρ = 0.976 with median swap price impact of 0.35%.

I prove that single-pool positions converge to equal value under repeated rebalancing (Theorem 2). A V/L sweep experiment confirms this empirically: positions deployed at ratio 1:3:9 collapsed to 1.37:1:1.20 within 33 events, with the original size ordering reversed. Multi-pool portfolios settle at position-specific equilibria determined by pool depth. Token-level decomposition across ten pools and five depositor groups reveals the Connector Rule. The siphon driver per pool is the token shared with more portfolio positions, and the same pool exhibits different driver tokens depending on the portfolio's topology.

I prove that positions which rebalance without executing a swap (S = 0) decay geometrically: V_K ≤ V₀(1 − α_min)^K where α_min > 0 is the minimum residual fraction per rebalance (Theorem 3). This result follows from the CL amount equations, the min() constraint in the liquidity-from-amounts function, and the finiteness of the shared dust pool. The theorem is verified with four additional Foundry tests (7/7 total) and validated against the complete lifecycle of a USDC/ZARP position that lost 99.8% of its capital ($942 → $1.59) in 14 zero-swap rebalances over 65 hours.

title: Architectural Recklessness: Why Black Box AI Is a Corporate Crime by Design

detail.title: Architectural Recklessness: Why Black Box AI Is a Corporate Crime by Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Myself

detail.abstract: As autonomous and semi-autonomous artificial intelligence systems transform from auxiliary systems to primary decision-making systems, they create a considerable "Accountability Gap" in corporate criminal law. Existing attribution theories, such as the Identification Principle and Vicarious Liability, are still based on 20th-century thinking, which assumes corporate crime can be attributed to a human "directing mind." However, the inherent "Black Box" nature of AI systems, in which decision-making processes cannot be explained even to the AI's creators, breaks this chain of intent. When AI optimization results in corporate crime, such as fraud, market manipulation, or criminal negligence, the "un-foreseeability defense" is used to externalize risk, turning AI's inherent opacity into a corporate shield against accountability. This article will demonstrate that this problem requires a fundamental shift in corporate criminal law from a focus on human intent to a "Systemic Culpability" based on "Architectural Recklessness." This involves shifting corporate criminal liability from the act of commission to the act of deployment. This article will propose that a corporation is guilty of criminal recklessness when it knowingly deploys an opaque, unexplainable, or uncontrollable AI system in a vital corporate function in which criminal harm is a reasonable, expected, or predictable outcome.

detail.abstract: Global supply chain operations are being affected by the digital technologies, which enhance the coordination, transparency, and efficiency of the operations. The current supply chains of logistics are getting more dependent on artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, and automated warehouse systems to manage the complex international supply networks. Such technologies enable organisations to make large amounts of operational data, enhance the predictability of demands, and track logistics operations in real-time. Nevertheless, the growth of the use of digital technologies also needs efficient leadership to guide the organisational change and promote the cooperation of human employees and automated systems. This study will look into how digital leadership is going to enhance the efficiency of operations in global supply chains. The research employs the secondary research method and evaluates the current scholarly sources concerning artificial intelligence, digital supply chains, and supply chain automation. Thematic analysis is employed to find out the key themes concerning AI fuelled operational efficiency, IoT powered supply chain visibility, warehouse automation, human technology cooperation, and digital leadership practices. The results have shown that digital technologies to a great extent enhance efficiency in logistics, transparency in supply chains, and operational decision making. Nevertheless, the efficient realization of these technologies is based on efficient digital leadership that facilitates adaptation to the workforce and the integration of technologies. The paper concludes that the digital leadership approach is crucial in managing technology enabled supply chain systems as well as guaranteeing sustainable operational performance.

title: When Fan Subscriptions Get Expensive: How Platform-initiated Price Changes Affect Creator Behavior and Viewer Spending
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst - Department of Marketing, University of Texas at Dallas and Southern University of Science and Technology

detail.title: When Fan Subscriptions Get Expensive: How Platform-initiated Price Changes Affect Creator Behavior and Viewer Spending
detail.abstract: Digital creator platforms increasingly rely on fan subscriptions as a creator-centric and recurring monetization channel, yet little is known about how platform-initiated pricing changes in fan subscriptions affect creator effort and viewer spending in environments with multiple coexisting revenue streams. We study Twitch's sudden subscription price increase in Turkey as a quasi-natural experiment. Using rich streamer-day panel data and a difference-indifferences design comparing Turkish streamers with matched streamers in Argentina, we find that the price increase reduces content provision: streaming frequency falls by 9.6% and airtime by 7.4%, despite higher subscription revenue. Further analysis shows that these reductions are concentrated among creators with higher accumulated subscription revenue and larger follower bases, consistent with a labor-leisure interpretation with strong income effects. On the demand side, viewer spending responds heterogeneously within the fan subscription channel: low-tier and gifted subscriptions decline sharply, whereas high-tier and nongifted subscriptions remain stable. Notably, we find no evidence of cross-channel substitution: virtual tipping and viewership-based advertising revenue remain unchanged. These results show that fan subscriptions function as a relationship-driven monetization channel whose pricing propagates through creator platforms by reshaping creator labor supply and reallocating demand within the fan subscription channel, rather than by inducing substitution across monetization channels.

title: Bottleneck Analysis in Industrial Manufacturing Systems: A Comparative Case Study of Ethiopia and Poland

detail.title: Bottleneck Analysis in Industrial Manufacturing Systems: A Comparative Case Study of Ethiopia and Poland
detail.abstract:
Bottleneck analysis is a widely used method for identifying constraints that hinder system productivity and limit process efficiency. Thus, this research aims to shed light on the results of such analysis in two regions with notable differences in various elements. These differences contribute to the types of bottlenecks, the methods implemented to address them, and the relief of the bottlenecks. 


The data collection used in this research is of two types. The first was primary data collection through field observation, interviews, and production logs with an industrial filler manufacturing company in Ethiopia. The second type of data collection used was secondary data collection with the Polish company, using the article “The Case Study of Bottlenecks Identification for Practical Implementation to the Theory of Constraints” to make the comparison. 


From the research, we can observe that in both countries, there was a substantial improvement in time efficiency. In Ethiopia, rigid systems that didn’t allow for process-level data led to machinery replacement and personnel incentive adjustments, which increased output from about 10 metric tons to 30-40 tons per shift. However, the Polish company's analysis was much more detailed, so we were able to solve the bottlenecks without investing in machine replacement, but rather by identifying wasted time through bottleneck analysis and reducing it. 


Both companies were affected by contextual constraints, which influence both the identification of bottlenecks and the feasibility of corrective actions. This suggests that bottleneck analysis must be adapted to local operational constraints to be effective.

title: Cross-Cultural Management Challenges in the International Semiconductor Market

detail.title: Cross-Cultural Management Challenges in the International Semiconductor Market
detail.abstract: The semiconductor industry functions in the hyper-internationalised production networks in which the western technology companies are partners with the Asian manufacturing companies. Nonetheless, cultural diversities among organisations can affect organisational managerial decision making, communication behaviours and results of partnerships. This paper explores the cross cultural management issues in the international semiconductor business by investigating the ways in which the cultural differences affect the cooperation between Western technology companies and the Asian semiconductor manufacturers. The study uses qualitative research design guided by the secondary data gathering and qualitative analysis via thematic analysis. Literature on the subject of academics, industry reports and international business studies were analyzed to establish key cultural themes that drive international technology alliances. The results indicate that there are a number of cultural issues that affect semiconductor partnerships. Power distance affects the hierarchical decision making systems within the Asian organisations as western companies favour decentralised systems of running the company. Individualism and collective orientation also have an influence on the negotiation behaviour and organisation of operations between partner firms. The uncertainty avoidance differences affect the way risks are mitigated and strategies of technology development. Asian organisations have long term orientation which promotes stable relationships between partnerships, and the Western firms tend to focus more on short term performance of the market. Knowledge sharing and international collaboration between international teams is also influenced by differences in communication style. This paper concludes that global semiconductor collaborations need culturally sensitive leadership and cross cultural management skills in order to enhance the level of cooperation.

detail.abstract:
The thesis forms the foundation of the DNFM through a mixed-methods design comprising a survey with 199 respondents, 108 employee stakeholder narratives, 15 participants in an exploratory experiment, and multiple expert interviews.

Key findings reveal that feedback is perceived as most ethical when it is developmental at its core rather than evaluative, concrete, clear, and fair. Across multiple methods, the same result emerges: feedback from a virtue-ethical transformational manager is considered the best, based on moral norms, with important concepts such as psychological safety and ownership. These concepts are checked and compared with the literature. Statistical analysis showed that quality and ethics correlated strongly, highlighting the importance of developing substance and supporting the need for profound changes in communication.

By integrating leadership theories, metaethical-to-normative frameworks, applied psychology, and business theories with newly discovered insights, the DNFM is proposed. The model emphasises flexibility, actionability, managerial duties, and continuous ethical calibration. Practical recommendations and actionable plans are formulated for Dutch knowledge-based teams. The Dynamic Normative Feedback Model (DNFM) fills the research gap by adopting a distinct approach to current Dutch practices. It provides a broader framework, especially when it comes to ethical demands and integrating multidisciplinary approaches.

title: Optimality-Induced Stabilization in Stochastic Networked Resource Allocation Systems

detail.title: Optimality-Induced Stabilization in Stochastic Networked Resource Allocation Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.

detail.abstract: Large-scale operational systems such as transportation, logistics, and distributed service networks must allocate limited resources under stochastic demand while maintaining stable system performance. These systems are often modeled as stochastic network optimization problems in which resource allocation decisions are chosen to minimize congestion or operational costs subject to shared capacity constraints. While classical scheduling policies enforce stability through explicitly designed control rules, many real-world decision systems rely primarily on cost-driven optimization mechanisms. This paper investigates whether cost-minimizing policies can inherently guarantee stability in stochastic networked resource allocation systems. We study a class of controlled Markov decision processes with convex capacity regions and coercive congestion cost functions. We prove that when the exogenous demand vector lies strictly within the interior of the capacity region, every optimal stationary policy for the discounted problem necessarily induces a negative Foster-Lyapunov drift outside a compact set, implying positive recurrence of the system state. Conversely, when demand exceeds the capacity boundary, no feasible policy can stabilize the system, establishing the convex capacity region as the maximal stabilizable demand set. The theoretical results are illustrated through computational experiments on a multi-terminal logistics network with stochastic arrivals and shared routing capacities. Simulation results reveal a clear phase transition between stable and unstable regimes and demonstrate that convex congestion-based optimization policies can reproduce the stabilizing behavior of classical scheduling rules while achieving lower operational costs. These findings highlight a structural link between economic optimization and stochastic stability in networked operational systems.

title: The Surprising Virtues of Heterogeneity: Legal Pluralism and the Governance of Generative AI
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University, Dickinson Law

detail.title: The Surprising Virtues of Heterogeneity: Legal Pluralism and the Governance of Generative AI
detail.abstract: This Article argues that the United States' fragmented approach to generative AI regulation is a strategic strength rather than a flaw. In place of a single federal regime, privacy law, the right of publicity, and copyright offer overlapping tools to address identity-linked harms, each grounded in distinct theories of harm and institutional traditions. This pluralism promotes experimentation, learning, and well-reasoned development rather than confusion. Heterogeneous governance helps courts and lawmakers adapt incrementally to fast-moving technologies, avoid premature lock-in, and coordinate protections across legal silos. To build on these advantages, the Article proposes a narrowly tailored data right focused on high-fidelity, identity-linked uses of data. Functioning as an opt-in, transparency-driven supplement to existing doctrines, this right would close gaps while preserving innovation and doctrinal diversity. The result is a principled, pragmatic approach that safeguards individual agency and leverages the adaptive strengths of US federalism.

detail.abstract:
This technical note provides an overview of accounting for accounts receivable. Students will learn how to account for sales on account, record write-offs and recoveries of accounts receivable, and estimate of bad debt expense using both the aging method and percent of sale method.

Excerpt

Accounting for Accounts Receivable and Bad Debt Expense

When companies sell their products and services, they often do not receive cash from their customers right away. Instead, the companies may provide their customers with a short buffer to make payments, allowing them to purchase on account. When this option is taken, a company records relevant transactions in its Accounts Receivable account.

Companies sell on account to increase sales, as customers may be more likely to make purchases if they can delay payment to a later date. But selling on account has costs. It delays the receipt of cash, the company incurs costs to send bills and collect from customers, and some customers ultimately may not pay their bills. The managerial question for the seller is whether the increase in sales from selling on account more than offsets the costs associated with doing so.

Financial Reporting Considerations

When a company makes a sale on account, it records revenue and a corresponding receivable. The receivable is recorded as an asset on the balance sheet, as it (1) is owned or controlled by the company (i.e., the company has a right to receive payment) and (2) is expected to generate a future economic benefit (i.e., a future receipt of cash). The receivable recorded is the amount for which the company has an unconditional right to payment from the customer. The receivable remains on the books until the customer makes payment or until the company decides that account is uncollectible.

detail.title: Professional Obstacles: A Perception-Based Survey of Women Members of AO Trauma - Latin America
detail.abstract: Purpose: Orthopaedic surgery remains one of the most homogenous fields in medicine, with men accounting for over 95% of all orthopaedic surgeons worldwide. Regardless of age, experience, or academic achievement, women orthopedists have historically been underrepresented in leadership positions, academic medicine, and specialty societies and associations. While these trends are recognized globally, limited studies examine gender-based dynamics in Latin America. This perception-based survey aims to bring awareness to the experiences and challenges of women members of AO Trauma Latin America (AO T Lat).Methods: A questionnaire evaluating the experiences and challenges of women orthopedic surgeons was designed in collaboration with AO T Lat and several national Latin American orthopaedic societies. The questionnaire was divided into sections: demographics, motivations and opportunities, challenges and barriers, and AO-faculty-specific questions utilizing a 5-point Likert scale to rank items. The survey was distributed to women orthopaedic surgeons identified through AO T Lat, national orthopaedic societies, and professional networks throughout Latin America.Results: 116 women responded to the survey, representing current or former AO T Lat members from 16 Latin American countries. Intellectual stimulation and personal gratification and desire to work “hands-on” were the strongest motivators for specializing in orthopaedics (91%). Most respondents agreed with statements that they felt supported, included, and equal as women in AO Trauma, although there was a wide distribution of scores pertaining to these perceptions. Argentina, Colombia, Guatemala, and Mexico had sufficient respondents to evaluate statistically significant differences between these countries. The extent to which respondents felt included in their national AO chapter varied significantly between countries (p = 0.022), as did the perceived equality for faculty opportunities between men and women within the respondents’ country (p = 0.05).Conclusion: Perspectives expressed by women members of Latin America’s largest international orthopaedic trauma surgeon organization, AO T Lat, provide insight into their views on the support they receive and the biases they experience. Understanding these perceptions will assist in developing strategies for the continued diversification of the field of orthopaedic trauma, in Latin America and other regions globally.

title: Accounting for Intercorporate Equity Investments

detail.title: Accounting for Intercorporate Equity Investments
detail.abstract:
This technical note provides an overview of accounting for investments in equity securities. It discusses passive investments and fair value accounting, investments resulting in significant influence and the equity method of accounting, and investments resulting in control and consolidation accounting. It provides examples of each of the three possible accounting approaches and walks through the appropriate accounting for each.

Excerpt

Accounting for Intercorporate Equity Investments

Managers invest in other companies' securities for a variety of reasons. First, a company may have cash it would like to invest in the stocks or bonds of another company simply to generate a return. Second, a company may invest in another company so that it can influence that company's policies and performance. Third, a company may invest in another company to obtain control of that company.

The method used to account for investment in other corporations depends on the degree of influence or control the investing company has over the investee company due to the investment. From a financial reporting perspective, these diverse reasons result in three broad investment categories: (1) passive investments, (2) investments that result in significant influence, and (3) investments that result in control.

Passive Investments

Passive investments are investments in securities of another company simply for the purpose of earning a rate of return. They can include investments in debt and equity securities. Although there are exceptions, investments in equity securities (e.g., stocks) are considered passive investments if the investing company owns less than 20% of the outstanding voting shares of the investee. Note that since preferred stock is typically nonvoting stock, it is usually considered a passive investment.

title: Hedonic and Eudaimonic Happiness in Academic Productivity: A Conceptual and Bibliometric Review
affiliations: Universidad Panamericana and Universidad Panamericana

detail.title: Hedonic and Eudaimonic Happiness in Academic Productivity: A Conceptual and Bibliometric Review
detail.abstract: Building research teams that simultaneously achieve high levels of well-being and productivity represents a persistent challenge for contemporary universities. This preprint examines the relationship between academic productivity and happiness by distinguishing between hedonic and eudaimonic approaches to well-being. Drawing on literature from psychology, philosophy, management, and education, and supported by a focused bibliometric review of recent research on research productivity, the paper explores whether these two dimensions of happiness operate as substitutes, complements, or hierarchical drivers of scholarly output. The analysis suggests that hedonic well-being primarily supports short-term motivation and creativity, whereas eudaimonic well-being sustains long-term perseverance, resilience, and research quality. Integrating both dimensions appears crucial for fostering sustainable academic productivity. Practical implications are discussed for individual researchers and higher-education institutions seeking to balance performance expectations with human flourishing.

detail.title: Accounting for Owners' Equity
detail.abstract:
This technical note provides an overview of accounting for owners' equity. It discusses the concepts of common stock and preferred stock, as well as authorized, issued, and outstanding shares. It covers the accounting for issuances of stock, repurchases of stock (treasury stock), capital stock and additional paid in capital, and dividends. It touches briefly on comprehensive income and earnings per share.

Excerpt

Accounting for Owners' Equity

Owners' equity, also called shareholders' equity or stockholders' equity, consists of contributed capital and earned capital.

Contributed Capital

Contributed capital is capital that the company's shareholders have contributed. More specifically, it is the net of the funds received from issuing shares to shareholders and the funds paid to repurchase shares from shareholders. This component of owners' equity consists of two general classes of stock—common stock and preferred stock.

Common stock

Common stock represents basic ownership in an organization. Owners of common stock typically have voting rights, so they can participate in company decisions that require shareholder votes. In the event of the company's liquidation, though, they rank lower than creditors and preferred shareholders in receiving any proceeds.

title: The AI Chip Depreciation Debate
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: The AI Chip Depreciation Debate
detail.abstract:
In November 2025, hedge-fund manager Michael Burry, whose bet against subprime mortgages was dramatized in the 2015 movie The Big Short, accused the major technology companies of inflating earnings by extending depreciation schedules on AI hardware, calling it “one of the more common frauds of the modern era.” The case places students in the role of an analyst at an AI-focused investment fund who must evaluate Burry's thesis and prepare the fund's response to nervous investors. Preparing that response forces the protagonist through a series of increasingly consequential questions. What is depreciation, and why does it matter if it is a noncash charge? How much discretion do managers have over useful-life estimates under GAAP, and what happens to reported earnings when they exercise it? Can a chip that physically functions for a decade become economically obsolete in two years, and if so, what does the matching principle require? And if Burry is right that earnings are overstated, does that necessarily mean these stocks are overvalued? The case is designed for core financial accounting or financial statement analysis and valuation courses, with emphasis adaptable to each context.

Excerpt

The AI Chip Depreciation Debate

On the morning of November 11, 2025, Cecilia Chu arrived at the offices of Prometheus Capital (Prometheus) to find her colleagues clustered around a Bloomberg terminal. The previous evening, Michael Burry—the hedge-fund manager whose bet against subprime mortgages had been dramatized in the 2015 movie The Big Short—had broken a long public silence with a provocative claim: The major technology companies were “understating depreciation by extending useful life of assets,” a practice he labeled “one of the more common frauds of the modern era.”

For Prometheus, the accusation hit close to home. The firm had been founded in 2023 to capitalize on the AI boom, offering actively managed exposure to the companies building AI infrastructure. Its flagship fund held substantial positions in Microsoft Corporation (Microsoft); Alphabet Inc. (Alphabet); Meta Platforms, Inc. (Meta); and Oracle Corporation (Oracle)—precisely the “hyperscalers” (industry shorthand for the largest cloud infrastructure providers) that Burry was accusing of accounting manipulation. By noon, Chu had fielded three calls from nervous investors asking whether Prometheus needed to reassess its positions. She convened an informal meeting with two colleagues to discuss the fund's response.

Marcus Webb, who had joined Prometheus after 15 years as an investment banker, was dismissive. “Why does Burry even care about this? Depreciation isn't cash flow—it doesn't matter for valuing companies. All that matters is EBITDA. He's making noise about something that's irrelevant to investors.” Priya Sharma, who had come to Prometheus from a product management role at a cloud-computing start-up, looked puzzled. “I thought depreciation was basically a tax deduction—not a real expense. If Burry's saying these companies should take more depreciation, wouldn't that lower their taxes? Why would that be a problem?”
