title: The Financial Detective, 2026
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: The Financial Detective, 2026
detail.abstract:
This is an updated version of “The Financial Detective, 2016” (UVA-F-1763). This case presents the student with financial ratios for eight pairs of unidentified companies and asks them to match the description of the company with the financial profile derived from the ratios. The primary objective is to introduce students to financial ratio analysis—in particular, the range of ratios and the insights each one affords. The structured exploration of pairs of companies within an industry affords a number of important insights into strategy and financial performance. First, the economics of individual industries account for significant variations in financial ratios because of differences in technologies, product characteristics, or competitive structures. Second, financial performance results from managerial choices: Within industries, the wide variation in financial ratios is often a result of differences in corporate strategy in marketing, operations, and finance. For those reasons, this case is a good springboard into subsequent classes, which deal with the interaction of strategy and financial performance.

Excerpt

The Financial Detective, 2026

Financial characteristics of companies vary for many reasons. The two most prominent drivers are industry economics and firm strategy.

Each industry has a financial norm around which companies within the industry tend to operate. Because of the inherent capital intensity of the industry, a heavy goods manufacturer like automobiles or aircraft, for example, would naturally be expected to have a high proportion of fixed assets, while a consulting firm would not. Because of strong price competition, a discount retailer would be expected to have a lower gross margin than a pharmaceutical manufacturer that maintains highly differentiated products like patented drugs and enjoys more pricing freedom. Because of each industry's unique economic features, average financial statements will vary from one industry to the next.

Similarly, companies within industries have different financial characteristics, in part because of the diverse strategies that can be employed. Executives choose strategies that will position their companies favorably in the competitive jockeying within an industry. Strategies typically entail making important choices in how a product is made (e.g., capital intensive versus labor intensive), how it is marketed (e.g., through direct sales versus through distributors), and how the company is financed (e.g., using debt or equity). Strategies among companies in the same industry can differ dramatically. Different strategies can produce striking differences in financial results for firms in the same industry.

Their strategies and market niches provide clues as to the financial condition and performance that one would expect of them. title: Accounting for Revenues

detail.title: Accounting for Revenues
detail.abstract:
This technical note provides an overview of accounting for revenues. It discusses the five-step process to revenue recognition outlined in Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 606 and applies those steps to both a simple example of the sale by a bakery and a more complex example of the sale by a software company of a bundle of services.

Excerpt

Accounting for Revenues

Revenue is the increase in equity that a company generates from its normal business operations before subtracting expenses. It is one of the most important items reported in the company's financial statements. The amount of revenue and the growth in revenue over time indicate a company's success in placing its products or services in the hands of customers.

Revenue recognition refers to how much and when revenue is recorded by the company. Standard setters have articulated criteria to guide management's decisions on the amount and timing of revenue recognition. That said, deciding whether those criteria are met often requires judgment, so an element of subjectivity exists in the amount of revenue the company reports each period.

Sales of some products are straightforward, and the resulting decisions related to how much and when revenue should be recorded pose few challenges. Consider a customer who visits a supermarket to buy a loaf of bread. The customer chooses the bread, takes it to the self-checkout lane, scans its barcode, pays, and then leaves the supermarket with the loaf of bread they intend to consume throughout the upcoming week. The supermarket's revenue is the amount the customer paid for the loaf of bread, and that amount can be recorded as revenue immediately.

Other products and services can be more complicated and pose greater challenges to revenue recognition. Consider, for example, a software-as-a-service company whose sales frequently include software, consulting services, training, and other potential obligations, each of which might be offered over various time periods, and several of which might be bundled together at a total price lower than if each were purchased separately. In such situations, determining when to recognize how much revenue to record is less straightforward.

detail.title: Accounting for Property, Plant, and Equipment and Depreciation Expense
detail.abstract:
This technical note provides an overview of accounting for property, plant, and equipment and depreciation expense. It discusses determining what costs related to the asset should be capitalized and what should be expensed, determining what amount should be recorded on the income statement each period as depreciation expense (including alternative depreciation methods), determining if and when a change in the value of an asset should be recorded, and determining when to dispose of a fixed asset and how to reflect that in the financial statements.

Excerpt

Accounting for Property, Plant, and Equipment and Depreciation Expense

Property, plant, and equipment (PP&E), otherwise known as fixed assets, are long-lived, tangible assets that help generate a benefit (i.e., revenue) over multiple future periods. In contrast to inventory, which is purchased for resale, fixed assets are purchased to help the company make and deliver products and services that it sells to generate revenue. Due to their nature, they are often one of the largest assets on a company's balance sheet.

When a company acquires a new fixed asset, the value is recorded as an asset on the balance sheet, as it (1) is owned or controlled by the company and (2) is expected to generate a future economic benefit. More specifically, it is a noncurrent asset since it is expected to generate a benefit for multiple years. The PP&E account on the balance sheet generally includes property (e.g., land), plant (e.g., buildings), and equipment (e.g., machinery, production and office equipment, and furniture).

Financial Reporting Considerations

Managers must make several business and accounting decisions related to PP&E. These can include:

Determining what costs related to the asset should be capitalized (i.e., recorded on the balance sheet as assets) and what should be expensed (i.e., recorded as expenses on the income statement).

title: Katni Fibres, Ltd
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Katni Fibres, Ltd
detail.abstract:
In January 2025, the chief executive of a small yarn-production company in India must resolve an unexpected cash shortage. The task for the student is to evaluate the causes of this shortage (using a completed “base-case” forecast given in the case) and assess the usefulness of various possible remedies suggested by managers in the company. In essence, the company is unable to zero out a seasonal working-capital loan for the requisite 30 days each year. This difficulty arises from two classic causes: secular growth of the company and declining profitability. Possible remedies include reducing inventory through more efficient transportation and warehousing, reducing credit terms to customers, switching from seasonal to level production, improving profitability, decreasing dividends, and reducing sales growth. The case is an updated and simplified version of an antecedent case, Kota Fibres, Ltd. (UVA-F-1359). At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this case is used in the core MBA finance curriculum in a module on financial forecasting.

Excerpt

Katni Fibres, Ltd.

Surabhi Kumar, managing director and principal owner of Katni Fibres, Ltd. (Katni), discovered the problem when she arrived at the company's plant one morning in early January 2025. Customers for whom rolls of fiber yarn were intended had been badgering Kumar to fill their orders in a timely manner, yet trucks that had been loaded just the night before were being unloaded because the government tax inspector, stationed at the company's warehouse, would not clear them for departure. The excise tax had not been paid: The inspector required a cash payment, but in seeking to draw funds that morning, Vikram Malik, the bookkeeper, had discovered that the company had overdrawn its bank account—for the third time in as many weeks. The truck drivers, who were independent contractors, cursed loudly as they unloaded the trucks, refusing to wait while the company and government settled their accounts.

This shipment would not leave for at least another two days, and angry customers would no doubt require an explanation. Before granting a loan with which to pay the excise tax, the branch manager of the All-India Bank & Trust Company (All-India) had requested a meeting with Kumar for the next day to discuss Katni's financial condition and its plans for restoring its liquidity.

Kumar told Malik, “This cash problem is most vexing. I don't understand it. We're a very profitable enterprise, yet we seem to have to depend increasingly on the bank. Why do we need more loans just as our heavy selling season begins? We can't repeat this blunder.”

title: Sun River Electronics Ltd
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Sun River Electronics Ltd
detail.abstract:
In July 2025, a new CEO joins Sun River Electronics Ltd., a small microphone manufacturer, to discover that the firm is in the midst of a financial crisis that was induced by rapid growth. The CEO asks an analyst for help with five tasks: (1) review the historical performance of the firm, (2) forecast financing requirements for the next two years, (3) exercise the forecasting model to identify key driver assumptions, (4) estimate Sun River's weighted average cost of capital, and (5) analyze a proposed investment in a packaging machine. The analyst must offer insights and recommendations based on the work.This relatively short case poses several review-type problems for the students. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, it is designed to be taught over two consecutive class periods in the first-year MBA finance course. It has also been used as a midcourse five-hour exam in that course.

Excerpt

Sun River Electronics Ltd.

On July 25, 2025, her first day as CEO of Sun River Electronics Ltd. (Sun River), Mei Ling Lim confronted a host of management problems. One week earlier, Sun River's president and CEO had suddenly resigned to accept a CEO position with another firm. Lim, a principal at New Era Partners (New Era), an Asian venture-capital firm, had been appointed to fill the position—starting immediately.

Several of the issues that had surfaced that first day were financial in nature, either requiring a financial decision or with outcomes that would have major financial implications for the firm. To make progress on these issues, Lim met with her assistant, Andy Chin, to begin addressing the most prominent ones.

Sun River Electronics Ltd. and the Microphone-Manufacturing Industry

Sun River resulted from a joint venture between major British electronics company Sunlight Ltd. (Sunlight) and New Era. Based in Singapore, Sun River had a single business mission: to efficiently manufacture quality microphones for large-scale commercial and retail consumers.

When it was originally founded, Sun River had gained early recognition for its cost-efficient production of condenser microphones. The condenser (or capacitor) microphone technology had been around since the early 1900s, when it was invented by Edward “E. C.” Wente at the American electrical engineering and manufacturing firm Western Electric Company. The innovation involved capturing sound pressure created by the movement of a thin membrane and converting the vibrations into electrical output. Now, in the 2020s, as demand for small-scale microphone capability continued to grow, Sun River was a market leader in manufacturing quality small-format microphones and microphone parts on a cost-efficient basis.

detail.title: Revenue Recognition at Salesforce.com, Inc
detail.abstract:
This case, adapted from "Revenue Recognition (Topic 606) at Salesforce.com, Inc." (UVA-C-2428), uses an array of carefully selected and excerpted revenue-recognition related information contained in Salesforce, Inc.'s (Salesforce's), 2025 SEC Form 10-K. Jessica, the fictional protagonist, is seeking to understand those disclosures as part of her preparation for an upcoming job interview with the company. She is relying on those disclosures to provide insights as to the company's main product and service lines, the events that signal when and how much revenue the company has earned (i.e., the essence of its business model), along with the related official generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) criteria pertinent to the valuing and timing of recorded revenues.

Excerpt

Revenue Recognition at Salesforce, Inc.

Jessica eagerly anticipated her upcoming interview with Salesforce, Inc. (Salesforce). With a week or so to prepare before heading to San Francisco for her on-site interview, she decided to assemble some information from the company's most recent Form 10-K, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). In particular, she recalled learning in her accounting course that a company's revenue-recognition practices and related financial disclosures offered a helpful glimpse into a company's business model. Wanting to be well versed on that for her interview, she gathered the company's financial statements and important revenue-related information presented in the footnotes to those financial statements and included in the 10-K.

When the topic of revenue recognition had been covered in her accounting course, Jessica had been intrigued by the Financial Accounting Standards Board's (FASB's) latest revenue-recognition and disclosure requirements. The FASB issued comprehensive new revenue-recognition guidance and several follow-on intrpretations and addendums (published as Accounting Standard Codification [ASC] 606, but often referred to as “Topic 606”), largely intended to clarify what companies could do in reporting revenues for fiscal years 2018 and later. Prior to this guidance, companies had to consider various revenue-recognition rules from various sources, which sometimes had ambiguous or even contradictory requirements. In addition, Jessica had learned that many of the known financial reporting misstatements or frauds in the recent past were related to the misreporting of revenues. Generally, guilty companies had been too aggressive in recording more revenues sooner than they should have. Indeed, the new guidance in Topic 606 was expected to be impactful: “The new accounting rules are considered by many to be the biggest change to accounting standards in the last 100 years. Noncompliance is a huge risk. Revenue recognition errors are the biggest reason for earnings restatements. Earnings restatements can lead to firings, fines, and even jail time.”

title: Bargaining Under Bilateral Monopoly
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Bargaining Under Bilateral Monopoly
detail.abstract:
This technical note introduces the economics of bilateral monopoly, a market structure in which a single seller faces a single buyer. Unlike competitive markets, bilateral monopoly produces no unique equilibrium price; instead, it generates a range of mutually beneficial outcomes, the contract zone, whose boundaries are determined by each party's outside options. The note explains why standard supply-and-demand analysis cannot predict the settlement within this range and examines the forces that shape it: threat points and how they shift with changing alternatives, focal points and precedent as coordination devices, self-serving bias as a source of disagreement over fairness, asymmetric information as a cause of avoidable impasse, and strategic delay as a costly signaling mechanism. The note builds on the competitive market framework presented in "The Economics of Competitive Markets" (UVA-GEM-0180) and the monopoly analysis in "Imperfect Competition and Monopolies" (UVA-GEM-0105). It is designed for use in MBA electives covering sports economics, labor economics, or negotiation, and pairs well with cases involving collective bargaining, supply chain negotiations, or merger transactions.

Excerpt

Bargaining Under Bilateral Monopoly

In most markets, prices emerge from the interaction of many buyers and many sellers. A wheat farmer takes the market price as given; so does the consumer at the grocery store. But some of the most consequential economic transactions occur in settings where this competitive logic breaks down: A single buyer faces a single seller, and no market mechanism determines the price. Labor negotiations between a players' union and a professional sports league, wage bargaining between a firm and its workforce, and contract disputes between a sole-source supplier and its only customer all share this structure.

This note describes the economics of bilateral monopoly, a market structure in which one buyer faces one seller. It explains why standard supply-and-demand analysis fails in such settings, why the resulting price is indeterminate within a range, and how negotiators use precedent and focal points to coordinate expectations. The note also addresses why negotiations sometimes break down even when mutually beneficial agreements exist.

Bilateral Monopoly and the Bargaining Range

A bilateral monopoly exists when a single seller (a monopolist) faces a single buyer (a monopsonist). Unlike competitive markets, where the equilibrium price is determined by the intersection of supply and demand curves, bilateral monopoly produces no unique equilibrium. Each side has a preferred outcome: The seller would like to charge the monopoly price; the buyer would like to pay the monopsony price. But neither side can unilaterally impose its preferred terms, and the final price will fall somewhere between them.

What determines the boundaries of the feasible range? Each party's limit is set by its reservation value or “walk-away” point, the payoff from its best alternative if negotiations fail. The seller will not accept any price below what it could obtain elsewhere; the buyer will not pay more than the value of its next-best option. The set of outcomes that both parties prefer to their respective reservation values is the contract zone (Figure 1). Any agreement within this zone is mutually beneficial, but which point the parties actually reach remains indeterminate.

title: Rocksmith Machine Tools: Artificial Intelligence and the Dividend Decision
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Rocksmith Machine Tools: Artificial Intelligence and the Dividend Decision
detail.abstract:
In mid-September 2025, Emily Ray, the CFO of Rocksmith Machine Tools Corporation, a large computer-aided design and manufacturing equipment manufacturer, needs to decide whether to pay out dividends to the firm's shareholders or to repurchase stock. If Ray chooses to pay out dividends, she will also have to decide upon the magnitude of the payout. A secondary question is whether the firm should embark on a campaign of corporate-image advertising and change its corporate name to reflect its new outlook.The case serves as a review of the many practical aspects of dividend and share-buyback decisions, including (1) signaling effects; (2) clientele effects; and (3) the finance and investment implications of increasing dividend payouts and share-repurchase decisions. This case can follow a treatment of the Miller–Modigliani dividend-irrelevance theorem and serves to highlight practical considerations to bear in mind when setting a firm's dividend policy.This is an updated version of UVA-F-1765. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this case has been successfully used in the core MBA finance course.

Excerpt

Rocksmith Machine Tools: Artificial Intelligence and the Dividend Decision

On September 15, 2025, Emily Ray, CFO of Rocksmith Machine Tools Corporation (Rocksmith), paced the floor of her Minnesota office. She needed to submit a recommendation to Rocksmith's board of directors regarding the company's dividend policy, which had been the subject of an ongoing debate among the firm's senior managers. Ray knew that the board tended to be optimistic about Rocksmith's future, but they also appreciated that operating in a competitive and dynamic industry was filled with uncertainty. They had experienced the past few turbulent years when Rocksmith's revenue had refused to grow and its profit margins had languished. Now, after two significant company restructurings, the expectation was for financial improvement and increased share of the global computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM) market.

There were two issues that complicated Ray's dividend policy recommendation. First, over the past three years, Rocksmith shareholders had experienced no capital gain (i.e., the current stock price of $15.25 was essentially unchanged since September 2021). The only return shareholders had received was dividends, which amounted to an average annual return of 2.9% and compared poorly to the annual return of 8.8% earned by the average stock over the same period. The second complication was that the recent stock price volatility had prompted a number of companies to repurchase shares either in lieu of or in addition to paying a dividend. A share repurchase was considered a method for management and the board to signal confidence in their company and was usually greeted with a stock price increase when announced. Rocksmith had repurchased $15.8 million of shares in 2019, but it had not used share buybacks since then. Ray recognized, therefore, that her recommendation needed to include whether to use company funds to buy back stock, pay dividends, do both, or do neither.

detail.title: Firm Data on AI

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We present the first representative international data on firm-level AI use. We survey almost 6,000 CFOs, CEOs, and executives from stratified firm samples across the US, UK, Germany, and Australia. We find four key facts. First, around 70 percent of firms actively use AI, particularly younger, more productive firms. Second, while over two-thirds of top executives regularly use AI, their average use is only 1.5 hours a week, with one quarter reporting no AI use. Third, firms report little impact of AI over the last three years, with more than 80 percent of firms reporting no impact on either employment or productivity. Fourth, firms predict sizable impacts over the next three years, forecasting AI will boost productivity by 1.4 percent, increase output by 0.8 percent, and cut employment by 0.7 percent. We also survey individual employees who predict a 0.5 percent increase in employment in the next three years as a result of AI. This contrast implies a sizable gap in expectations, with senior executives predicting reductions in employment from AI and employees predicting net job creation.
